speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should say that I propose first to call the resolutions on the Customs Tariff, then on the Excise Tax, and then on the Income Tax.
So far as the Customs Tariff changes are concerned, I would like to refer back to my budget speech when I mentioned that with the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations taking place in Geneva I was proposing few changes in the Customs Tariff this year.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
It might help the members of the committee if I were to make some very general remarks about them.
There are four resolutions relating to the Customs Tariff. The first and second resolutions provide for amendments to schedules A and B of the Customs Tariff and contain 18 tariff items. Some of the items are new and for some the coverage is being broadened, while others are merely being continued without change for a further period. The third resolution provides for a technical amendment to an item in schedule C of the Customs Tariff, and schedule C lists the goods which are prohibited entry. The fourth resolution deals with the coming into force of the three previous resolutions.
That is all I have to say by way of general comment on the structure of the changes that are being proposed and perhaps at this point I should sit down and respond to questions.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we are dealing with Customs Tariff resolutions of the type we have before us they seem to receive relatively little attention from the house and the communications media. I do not understand why it is that there is great attention
June 7. 1966

paid by commentators and writers of editorials to budgets. There is always a great buildup before the delivery of a budget and a great amount of coverage given immediately following its delivery, but when we come to studying the items contained in detail in the budget, members of the communications media all leave and we see very little if anything written about that study. If one wants to clear this house of people involved in the field of communications one need only speak about budget resolutions and the bills that follow those resolutions. Yet everyone is affected by them.
For many years I have worked on budgets on both sides of this house; yet when I spoke it seemed as though I were almost conducting a monologue, along with a few others including the Minister of Finance. This is an astounding fact when we consider that under the Customs Tariff Act the government receives 9 per cent of its revenue, which is not inconsiderable in relation to attempted raids by provincial governments on the general revenues of the government of Canada. During a recent political campaign certain people asserted that matters coming under the Customs Tariff should be the subject of a dialogue between the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces. In fact, some went so far as to say that trade, and I presume that included matters associated with trade such as customs tariffs, should be the prerogative of the provinces. Of course, I have never heard such utter nonsense in my life.
This country was founded on a constitution which set forth that there should be no obstruction to trade by the provinces. If provinces got their hands on customs tariffs or the deliberations as to customs tariffs or matters of trade we would see the greatest chauvinistic policies ever followed. If ever there was a move to balkanize Canada it would come as the result of moves toward changing jurisdiction in respect of acts such as the Customs Tariff Act.
Let us look at what the minister has proposed in respect of customs tariffs. This year the minister was wise enough to say that he did not propose to do very much in light of negotiations under the Kennedy round. I suggest that the minister proposes to do nothing because nothing happened under the Kennedy round. As a matter of fact, the progress made under that round of talks prior to the delivery of the minister's budget speech was almost nil. In fact, progress, if anything, was retrograde.
Customs Tariff
When we look at the items contained in the budget, other than those which deal with the automobile agreement which are tied in with sales tax on machinery for the purpose of auto parts manufacturing, we find there is precious little in the over-all that really affects Canada's customs tariff. Let us look at the items in relation to Canada's economy. What does "Feeds for use exclusively in the feeding of trout, on and after July 1, 1968" mean? There is also a reference to July 1, 1966, but what does this actually mean in terms of the economy?
Although the next item may be of interest to the individuals who are concerned, what will the change in "carnation cuttings in their first year of introduction" mean in terms of our economy? There is another item which I suppose will have some effect on small people. It relates to liquorice blocks, granules, paste or powder, not sweetened. What will that mean in terms of the economy?
Then we go from the sublime to the ridiculous in terms of these tariff items. Without casting any reflection on any business that may be connected with this item, move from liquorice blocks to captive balloons having a volume of 150,000 cubic feet or more which are to be used in the logging industry. The members of this house will require some education in this field because I am sure very few here know what this type of equipment is or how it is used. Are these balloons hung onto a mountainside from which a boom is suspended hauling logs out of inaccessible areas? In any event, I am sure that this change will not cost the crown a great deal of money because the use of captive balloons in this industry must be somewhat restricted.
The items also include a number of chemicals and minerals that are again of a kind which are used to a lesser degree than others. There is reference also to guns and rifles of a class or kind not made in Canada, parts thereof. Then there is an item for "oriental rugs or carpets with pile hooked or knotted by hand". This may have some appeal to those with aesthetic tastes, and the minister may want to point out the particular trade agreement under which the tariff reduction on this item was decided. There is a substantial reduction in the tariff here. Again, I think we would want an explanation from the minister as to how he is going to amend the regulations governing a settler's effects. Will this have to do with automobiles and an increase in the valuation of a settler's effects? Before

the resolution is passed we should have some indication from the minister in this regard.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Last year and the year before-when I was on the government side I spoke privately to the then minister of finance about this matter-I wondered why items 44043-1 and 44047-1, dealing with aircraft engines of a particular size, were not incorporated on a permanent basis. I believe we have gone through the performance, in the nine years I have been in this house, of giving an annual extension to these particular items. How long is this to go on? Is this a sort of exclusive pragmatic approach? Those are the only remarks I shall make in regard to the particular items that appear under Customs Tariff resolution No. 1.
Resolution No. 2 deals with the question of drawback. This is a somewhat more important matter and I am sure other members of the house will wish to speak on it because it affects the operations of Canada's automobile industry under the automobile parts agreement when we see that there is introduced a 99 per cent drawback on "machines; precision instruments and apparatus for heat treating, welding, sorting, testing, inspecting or correcting; control panels for use with the aforementioned machines and precision instruments and apparatus; all of the foregoing of a class or kind not made in Canada; accessories", etc. The amendment is:
When used in the plants of manufacturers of automobiles and motor vehicles or of automobile or motor vehicle parts for the manufacture of automobiles and motor vehicles or of automobile or motor vehicle parts; or when used for the manufacture of dies, jigs, fixtures or moulds which are used in the production of automobile or motor vehicle parts.
In actual fact this amendment goes one step back of the actual manufacture or assembling of automobiles or parts therefor in that the minister is including dies, jigs and machine tools that go to make up these automobiles and parts. The comments of the hon. member for Wellington South and others on behalf of the opposition clearly indicated that this would provide some very special relief. I think the minister must be commended for making this change and trying to help our auto parts manufacturers to achieve a position of relative equality with their counterparts and competitors in the United States, because the American manufacturers do not have to pay a comparable sales tax. That amendment is introduced under the Excise
TMr. Lambert.]
Tax Act. There is also the relief from any duty under the Customs Tariff when these machines are not made in Canada. That is all well and good in the event that we want to make the auto parts agreement function in the best possible way.
The third item has to do with certain very important matters, namely, used or second hand mattresses or materials therefrom. I think the minister should enlighten the house why this particular item was negotiated. Was it on behalf of a particular industry? I could talk to the minister about other industries which have made representations as to tariff changes. I know that his officials have had correspondence for instance, with the manufacturers of drilling bits in Canada who are trying to found a small, albeit important, secondary industry in the Canadian oil industry. They are in competition with a much larger industry in the United States. They are in competition with, shall we say, much more entrenched business habits which are in fact restrictive agreements on the part of American manufacturers who have distributing agencies and branches in Canada which lay down restrictive marketing practices. A supply house in Canada, whether it be a branch supply house or an independent Canadian supply house, that wants to handle a particular type of drill bit manufactured in the United States cannot do so unless it agrees that the item will be handled exclusively. This make it very difficult for any Canadian business to get started in this field.
I want to draw to the minister's attention that there are many industries in the oil business in Canada to which in the past certain customs tariff relief has been given. I remember that some five or so years ago a plant producing sucker rods was given protection. This meant the difference between a large plant continuing in business or closing down completely. Fortunately the government of the day saw the wisdom of imposing a reasonable tariff compared with the American tariff. I believe we imposed a tariff of 10 per cent. The Canadian manufacturer could supply the North Dakota field and service it but in the face of a 22\ per cent United States duty.
A great many of these goods come in under a one-way flow. It is all very well to allow commodities to be imported into Canada free of duty, but try to do the same thing into the United States and one runs into a very high tariff wall. One might say that one of the incongruities of the Kennedy round of talks
June 7, 1966

is the offer to slash tariffs by 50 per cent in respect of certain commodities that may be negotiated. It is very well to say you will slash tariffs from 10 per cent to 5 per cent but this is not really meaningful if the countervailing American duty is 50 per cent or 37J per cent because cutting that one in half means that the tariff is still relatively very high. Therefore all of the proposals of the Kennedy round of talks have to be studied very carefully; they can be deceptive on the surface.
The next matter I wish to speak about is in the general nature of a discussion with regard to the Customs Tariff as it relates to surcharges and particularly British surcharges. We have read comments that the British government-this was disclosed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in his most recent budget declarations-proposes that by next November the British surcharges will have largely disappeared. It has been suggested in many quarters, and I would say informed quarters, that the reason these surcharges will be removed is that because of the pattern of British trade they really have not meant too much.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In fact, looking at today's headlines in the financial press one sees "pound hits 18 months' low point". There must be a very serious problem of imbalance of payments. If the pound is now down to the 18 months' low point it means that the customs surcharges are not having the effect of correcting the serious imbalance in British trade. Perhaps the minister will advise us on his thinking in this regard, although I am not inviting him to put himself in the role of the Chancellor of the Exchequer of the British Government. I am simply asking him to indicate to us his thinking on the nature of these surcharges.
He might also tell us what might be the effect on Canadian trade and Canadian customs of the devaluation of the Indian rupee. All these factors are affecting our trade. I realize that all these matters are partly under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. However, I am sure that the minister will take into account events which have come to pass since the Budget debate and, after listening to this discussion, will give us his views, because I believe the house and the country are entitled to know precisely what his thinking is in this regard.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Chairman, the Customs Tariff resolution is a relatively short one. The items are relatively inconsequential,

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one matter on which I want to ask the minister whether at some stage in the future he will consider making a statement to the house. I suppose that technically speaking it comes partly under the Department of Trade and Commerce but it is of such importance that perhaps the minister will take it into consideration.
I wish to say a few words about the Kennedy round of trade negotiations. When the trade expansion act was passed in 1962 it was greeted with wide acclaim and most parties in this house indicated an interest in it and a desire for Canada to participate. Recently, at the joint interparliamentary meeting in Washington, we had the opportunity to have some very frank discussions with members of the Senate and the House of Representatives concerning the Kennedy round of trade negotiations. Those discussions left us with the distinct impression that there is a very grave danger of the Kennedy round of negotiations ending in failure or becoming completely bogged down. Hon. members are certainly aware that a good deal of Canada's future trade and tariff policy is tied to the success of the Kennedy round.
The trade expansion act expires, I believe,, in June of next year, although I am not: positive of the date. The information which we received in Washington, and which we could not get here in Canada, was to the effect that the United States has not as yet been told by the European economic community the price which that community intends to set for the entry of U.S. agricultural products into Europe. This is really what the United States is after; they are primarily concerned with gaining access to the European economic community for their agricultural products. According to the United States people with whom we talked, a huge squeeze play is in progress. The European community is dragging its feet and has not yet told the U.S. the price it will demand. All the indications at present point to the fact that the European community will continue to do this until they run out the string, so to speak, until the trade expansion act has almost expired. They will then indicate to the United States the price which they intend to put on the entry of these U.S. products into

When that act was passed in 1962 nobody in the United States had any idea of the implications that the provision of the Kennedy round of negotiations might have on U.S. industry. In order to assuage the fears of many Americans the United States incorporated certain forms of adjustment and assistance in the trade expansion act. They were very vague but they were put in to allay fears in the United States regarding the imbalance which might result from actions taken under that act. Of course, in the interval there have been many test cases under this legislation and, as our U.S. friends told us, the legislation has not been successful and is not acceptable any more. Therefore once the renegotiation of the trade expansion act starts there will be a far greater amount of lobbying and pressuring in the U.S. than was the case in 1962. Fears were expressed to us that it will be very difficult to renew the trade expansion act in the same terms and that even if it is renewed, which is probable, the terms will be very different from those adopted in 1962.
I was very impressed with what the U.S. legislators told us. I felt that we got from them a greater degree of frankness and candour than we have been able to receive from successive ministers of trade and commerce here in Canada. We have received glib statements that the round is proceeding nicely and that everybody is happy, that Canada is sharing in frank discussions and that the outlook is bright. Yet when we spoke to the people responsible for the success of these talks we gathered from them that the outlook was one of pessimism and gloom for very obvious practical reasons.
That is why I hope that at some stage we will receive a frank statement from the government regarding its status in the negotiations. I realize that Canada is in a difficult position and that before the completion of negotiations between the United States and the European economic community it will be difficult for Canada to evaluate its position. However, I feel that to some extent we have been misled. There appears to be no second string to Canada's bow. We seem to have hitched our wagon to the success of this round of negotiations. This may not be the case and I would be very glad to have an indication to the contrary from the minister.

We have always been told since I first came to the house in 1962 that Canada's future trade patterns will embody a rationalization arising out of these negotiations. As I have indicated previously, the information we gathered from our talks in Washington was that the European economic community will keep the U.S. hanging in the air, will then tell them the price to be paid and then the squeeze play will begin in the United States to see whether or not the pressures at home are too great to permit renewal of the act. It seems to me this would pose great problems for Canada because of our dependence on U.S. trading patterns and our proximity to that country. I think that at some time in the future the business community in this country will be most interested in receiving a frank and realistic appraisal of the Kennedy round of negotiations.
Some of my colleagues will speak on other points in the Customs Tariff resolutions regarding such matters as carnations, trout and so on, which are not of great importance. However, there are some broader issues on which we hope to hear from the government at some time.

I have in my hand a letter dated December 29, 1965 over the signature of E. E. Burridge of the port administration branch, written to one of my constituents in answer to an inquiry he made. I should like to quote a part of it to indicate that my suggestion that some amendment is required is borne out by an
Customs Tariff
opinion of the national revenue department. The letter states in part;
As indicated in our previous letter the best possible treatment that may be accorded when an article is returned to Canada after being repaired in the United States is assessment of sales tax on only the value of the repair work. There is no provision in the customs law under which this assessment or payment of tax on repair parts may be waived. Any further relief from payment of tax would require a change in the legislation.
It seems to me, in a matter of this kind which obviously involves only a very minor change in the existing legislation, that on a purely humanitarian basis, if on no other, this is something which the minister might readily accept.
I am no authority on the ins and outs of entry documents but on the entry document in respect of this case there is listed "one carton-face respirator", and the tariff item applied is noted as being No. 41024-1. This document relates to the importation of a loan machine. It indicates that the arrangement is similar to what I stated earlier in that the levy is only $25. It also has on it the words, "authority for one-sixtieth entry attached." The tax exemption is allowed because of special circumstances relating to this being only a temporary importation.
It is my submission that in cases where machines of this kind are brought in on a temporary or loan basis or for that matter for the permanent use of a patient in Canada, a family desirous of importing such equipment should be on all fours with public hospitals. I cannot envisage any likelihood of abuse of this privilege by individuals inasmuch as no-one is going to want equipment of this kind unless he really requires it.
The importation of equipment for the purpose I have described could be authorized by hospital authorities who would indicate that the equipment was necessary. Would the minister indicate whether he is prepared to give some consideration to making this minor but very humane change in the customs law?

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three items which I would like to bring to the minister's attention, and perhaps when the minister makes his statement he might be kind enough to comment on my observations.
I think the terms of the resolution on excise tax which the minister is presenting are more to be criticized for their non-feasance than for their misfeasance. The items I wish to bring to the minister's attention are as follows. First of all, I think that perhaps most hon. members have had representations made to them at one time or another by various branches of the jewelery trade concerning the existing 10 per cent which is still levied on jewelry. I believe most hon members will perhaps agree that the retention of this tax on luxury items of jewelry may well be justified because these are items which should be taxed. However, there are a number of items in the jewelry trade which I would suggest are not in fact luxuries at all. I am now referring to inexpensive watches and items such as wedding and engagement rings. I suggest that the minister might well give careful consideration to removing the 10 per cent tax on watches and also on wedding and engagement rings below a certain value.
May I point out to the minister that this tax was levied during the last war. Since then the tax on luxury items has been reduced from 25 per cent to 10 per cent. On a great many luxury items such as furs, candy, firearms, golf clubs, fishing rods, cameras and projectors and many other articles which are clearly more in the nature of luxury items than inexpensive watches or wedding rings, the tax has been removed. I think the minister might give careful consideration to the removal of the tax on inexpensive watches and wedding and engagement rings below a certain value. I believe it can be safely said this would be of some benefit to the jewelry trade but it would also be of benefit to the average person who has to buy these articles which in fact are not luxury items.
There is another matter which I should like to bring to the minister's attention, the tax on materials used for centennial projects. I think many hon. members can probably cite a number of apparently anomalous situations. 
In my own constituency a public library was built as a centennial project and was exempted from tax. However, another project of a public nature was undertaken-I believe it was the building of a municipal hall-and in this case the tax was levied. Of course the reason for this is that public libraries are exempt from tax. However, I would think that when other buildings are being constructed as centennial projects they should also be exempted. This matter is very much in the people's minds these days because it is rather difficult to raise funds for these centennial projects. I therefore ask the minister to give consideration to removing the sales tax in the case of buildings which are constructed as centennial projects.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Another specific item of concern is a type of equipment being used for strictly agricultural purposes. This type of equipment, as most hon. members know, is the kind of equipment that has always caused trouble in individual cases because agricultural equipment is sometimes difficult to describe. In this instance I refer to a type of agricultural equipment which is imported and sold by a firm called Canadian Hydroponics Limited near the town of Tillsonburg, Ontario. The Department of National Revenue has had extensive correspondence with this company in this regard and it was held that the equipment would be taxable. This type of equipment can only be used for agricultural purposes since it produces, by means of hydroponics, certain fodder for cattle during the winter months. At one point this type of equipment was not subject to any sales tax because it was used in the production of other materials. After 1963, of course, this exemption was removed and it was again subject to sales tax.
Since this equipment is used particularly and exclusively for agricultural purposes and could not possibly be used for anything else, I request the minister to give consideration to exempting this specific item when the bill is presented. It is not the intention, as I understand it, of the legislation now in force that this kind of equipment should be subject to tax. As has happened many times in the past, equipment which is designed exclusively for and can only be used for agricultural purposes is being taxed simply because it does not come within the technical ambit of the legislation. I hope the minister will give consideration to this matter and include it in the appropriate budget bill.

First of all, when we consider the resolution in its entirety we see that parts of it are a companion to the Customs Tariff Act amendments particularly in relation to dies, jigs, fixtures, moulds, etc., which go into the manufacture of automobile parts or production machinery and for materials in connection with the manufacture of automobiles. There is also the withdrawal by the minister, effective April 1, 1967, of 5 per cent of the sales tax in so far as it affects both the Excise Tax Act and the Old Age Security Act. I do not know just how the combination is going to be effected in legislation. In any event, we see that over a number of items the sales tax is being entirely removed in relation to both acts.
If we go down the list of these particular items, naturally we come to the general classification of production machinery. This is all to the good. It shows that the minister has seen the benefits to the economy of the removal of this retrograde tax which was introduced in 1963. I suggest that the fact he has decided to remove it gradually is caused by the same general approach to the budget -do not do anything directly, just do it gradually. I do not know, but if he were worried about an increase in prices, as he should have been, he should have gone directly to the root cause of the government induced stimulus to prices which came about from 1963 onward. He should have gone, in this Budget, lock, stock and barrel after the whole of the 11 per cent sales tax in regard to production machinery.
Excise Tax Act
In so far as the effect on the automobile industry or the parts industry is concerned, I am going to leave some of my colleagues to deal with that. However, when I look over the items to which the reduction in sales tax is going to apply I am particularly struck by one item, and that is the type of commodity known as oil country goods. There is a restriction in the resolution saying, "all of the foregoing for use in connection with natural gas or oil wells", that is, "pipes or tubes commonly known as 'oil-country goods', being casing or tubing and fittings, couplings, thread protectors and nipples therefor", shall be subject to a tax reduction. However, I should like to ask, what about the production of oil from the bituminous tar sands? There is a $250 million refinery of a peculiar type being erected in Alberta which is due to come into production in 1967. It is true this company is not engaged in drilling for natural gas or oil but it certainly is using tubings, fittings, couplings, thread protectors and nipples therefor. They do not use drill pipes, at least not extensively to my knowledge.
Why, if this company is engaged in the production of crude oil, should it be placed at a disadvantage? I draw this to the minister's attention, and it may call for immediate study to see why this particular developing industry should be placed in a peculiar position. I am not going to ask for an immediate answer. I certainly ask the officials, both in the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue, to have a particular look at this segment of the oil industry and how it is to be affected by this provision.
There is one area in which I wish to commend the minister and the government because they have finally agreed there is nonsense in the distinction, which was imposed by the Department of National Revenue, continued I believe by the Tariff Board and, less understandably, the Exchequer Court, between natural gas which was used in internal combustion engines and that which was used in gas turbine engines, although destined for the same ultimate use, the production of energy. Those who were using gas turbines were denied the exemption from sales tax.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
There were bodies such as the city of Edmonton which had extensive retroactive assessments following rulings by the Tariff Board. There were also chemical concerns and utilities which were faced with this problem and which operated primarily in the

Alberta area. They found themselves with these retroactive assessments on the natural gas that they had been using following the ruling made by the Department of National Revenue.
May I say, Mr. Chairman, looking back upon the evidence of officials from the National Research Council and others, that how this artificial distinction between natural gas in an internal combustion engine and in a gas turbine was conceived and maintained would be completely beyond the comprehension of the members of this house. I am glad that the distinction has now been wiped out.
There is no provision in this resolution for any changes in the excise tax on liquor. Ever since I have been a member of the house the distilling industry has been putting forward briefs in regard to the amount of the excise tax and also the excise itself on alcohol. Merely to indicate the level that taxation has reached on this particular item and to indicate where it reaches its point of diminishing return, people have often said that if the Minister of Finance wants some more money he can tax liquor. If a province wants to increase its revenue it taxes liquor. This the provinces do, whether through their budgets or otherwise. I ran across some interesting information the other day. I am not making any particular brief here; I just want to put certain facts on record.
I am informed that in so far as the distiller is concerned he has made but one price increase since November 2, 1956. The increase on an in-bond basis since 1935 on premium priced whisky has been as little as $1.69 per case. That covers a period of over three decades. In 1935 the federal duty was $5.65 per case. Today it is $17.02 per case. Some people may suggest that the duty should be $37.02 per case. Others may suggest that it should be less than $7.02 per case. I am not going to argue this point; I merely draw to the attention of the committee the difference between the $5.65 in 1935 and the $17.02 in 1966. Then the provincial government adds on its mark-up and steps in with various sales taxes. The people who buy whisky should know just what goes into the cost of any given quantity of whisky.
To further heighten the tax burden the federal sales tax has increased from 6 per cent to 11 per cent or from $1.13 to $3.50 per case. In Ontario in 1935 the mark-up on laid-down cost was 51 per cent. Today, notwithstanding the very largely increased turnover, the mark-up is apparently 77 per cent.

I am sure that the various liquor control boards across the country are not far behind the province of Ontario in this regard. When it comes down to taxation of liquor, we know very well that every liquor control board takes its orders directly from the cabinet. They have nothing really to say about the over-all retail pricing of the commodities they sell. All that happens is that the provincial treasury determines how much revenue the liquor control boards of the province shall bring in. They are each assessed a certain revenue and on that basis the control boards set their prices. It is taxation quite directly but never with the approval of the legislature involved.
That is all I should like to say on that particular item, Mr. Chairman, by way of observation. The Minister of Finance of the government of Canada is, of course, much more straightforward in this regard. He is bound by the levels of taxation set out in the Excise Act and in the Excise Tax Act; not so the provinces.
There are a number of other minor items in the resolution on which I think not much need be said. However, there is one point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister, and I have drawn it to the attention of his colleague the Minister of National Revenue. It concerns a complaint I have received from many distributors of certain auto parts. Agricultural farm machinery as so classified today has many automotive parts which are absolutely interchangeable with those used in automobiles and farm motor trucks. I need not point out what happens. A farmer buys a replacement part ostensibly for a combine, say a carburetor or any part for a motor. Such things as spark plugs and other parts fit self-propelled farm machinery, trucks and even private automobiles.
If these parts are purchased for the repair of farm machinery they are not subject to sales tax. If they are purchased for the repair of automobiles or trucks they are subject to sales tax. So a loophole has been created. In all fairness, I must say I agree with the farmer who buys his parts ostensibly for use in farm machinery. If we consider that farm machinery should be exempt from sales tax, then so should the replacement parts. But let us not have any person who is entitled to buy sales tax exempt equipment and parts turn them aside for a use for which he should pay sales tax. This does affect the position of automobile parts distributors.

Mr. Chairman, in considering the excise tax resolution I want to deal with a particular aspect of the agricultural industry. This is a matter which I have referred to the minister and his predecessor. I am disappointed that it has not been dealt with in the resolution and I want briefly to recap the presentations I have made so that the minister will have an opportunity to consider and deal with them in the legislation following this resolution.
The change I am urging on the government is the provision of sales tax exemption for plastic netting used for the bailing of farm products. I refer particularly to the materials used in the Christmas tree industry. Currently, from my understanding of the law, sales tax exemption is provided for binder twine, wire, and other tying materials used in the bailing of farm products. Such exemption is not extended to the plastic netting used for bailing purposes in the Christmas tree industry.
The 11 per cent sales tax adds significantly to the cost of production for those using this type of material. I might say that it is a modern and new type of packaging which the government should take cognizance of and encourage.
I think I can best and in the shortest time outline this new innovation in the packaging industry by reading a descriptive release dealing with this matter which illustrates how it relates to the Christmas tree industry:
Several Canadian Christmas tree growers, hard pressed for manpower, are experimenting with a new wrapping method using plastic netting.
The new system will be used most extensively in the Pontypool, Ontario region, one of Canada's main growing areas. Growers there will use a simple funnel-like device developed by grower Sam Manetta of Pontypool. Several other devices using plastic netting are being developed in other areas.
By using the Manetta device, growers estimate they will wrap as many trees per day with three men as they formerly did with five, thus compensating for a shortage of harvesting labor. The tree is fed into the mouth of the funel and pulled through the neck. As the compressed tree emerges from the neck it is enveloped in a sleeve of plastic netting. No tying is involved. All experimental devices will accommodate any size of tree; the diameter of the sleeve varies with the tree size.
Excise Tax Act
In addition to increasing wrapping speed, the sleeve protects the tree from damage during loading and unloading by keeping all branches uniformly compressed. As a result, the frozen trees can be dragged or piled without danger of snapping off protruding branches. Trees packaged in plastic netting also present an attractive well-rounded package.
Growers in the Pontypool area concentrate on Scotch pine. Plantations cover thousands of acres- about 1,000 trees to the acre. Trees are shipped to all regions of Canada and the United States by tractor-trailer and railway.
I have mentioned the manpower shortage and the assistance that this type of packaging gives to the grower in the packaging of his trees. I want to mention briefly the considerable advantage to Canada accruing from the Christmas tree industry. In 1964 we exported over 9 million trees to the United States for about $6,200,000, thus providing a source of valuable foreign exchange. About 65 per cent of the trees grown in Canada go to the United States market.
May I also urge the government, in considering the amendment which I have requested in order to encourage this industry, to protect the industry against inroads being made by sales of artificial trees. In the United States artificial trees take over 35 per cent of the Christmas tree market.
That is all I can usefully say on this subject. I urge the minister to consider what I have said. Plastic netting ought to put the farmers and growers using it on the same basis as those using other materials to tie their produce. I hope that the minister will be able to include my suggestions in the legislation which will follow the adoption of this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose my main difficulty in accepting the minister's proposals at this point derives from a basic difference in our approach to the economy: what purposes the economy ought to serve and what purposes any steps taken in the fiscal field ought to serve. I suggest that one of the major difficulties about the kind of indirect, blunt instrument which the minister is using here, as elsewhere, to attempt to slow up investment is that it does harm in socially desirable areas irrespective of whether or not it does good in other areas.
I look, for example, at the proposal with regard to the gradual removal of the sales tax on certain machinery. I ask the minister, if I may, what value is there from the point of view of the productivity of our economy in retaining the sales tax at all?

June 7, 1966
Excise Tax Act
If I understood the minister's budget speech correctly, he said in effect that he had come to the conclusion that the sales tax on production machinery and equipment ought to be removed, but for the purpose of slowing down the tempo of the investment boom he felt that the removal ought to be gradual rather than immediate. I hope I have not misrepresented what he said.
I look at some of the machinery and equipment concerned and I ask the minister whether, in logic, encouraging employers, firms and businesses to purchase, instal and use such machinery and equipment now might not lead to a greater contribution to the economy and to a lowering of prices than the complicated business he has presented to us?
I look at paragraph 2 subparagraph (a) which read:
-machinery and apparatus sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers for use by them directly in the manufacture or production of goods.
Presumably we are dealing with the replacement of old, worn-out machinery by new machinery. Presumably no industrialist of any consequence will change machinery or buy new machinery or equipment or new apparatus unless the apparatus he has is inefficient.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I ask myself: By what investigation did the minister persuade himself that discouraging the purchase of machinery which could and would improve productivity would do good for the economy? I intend to read several of these items:
2(b) equipment sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers for use by them for exhausting dust and noxious fumes produced by their manufacturing or producing operations,
(c)	safety devices and equipment sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers for use by them in the prevention of accidents in the manufacture or production of goods,
(d)	equipment sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers for use by them in carrying refuse or waste from machinery and apparatus used by them directly in the manufacture or production of goods.
It is the same kind of thing all through. The machinery, equipment and apparatus listed and described in this resolution is machinery or apparatus which would improve the production process, in other words, it would result in improved productivity and a lower cost of production per unit. Surely this is the best way of improving the productivity of industry, to turn out goods which are needed on the one hand and to take steps

toward reducing unit costs of production on the other. Surely this could make a more important contribution toward lowering price levels or preventing them from increasing further, than the mere postponement of sales tax reductions would ever do.
If the minister's assumption that it is necessary to slow down the investment boom is correct, and if he is right that fiddling with the sales tax can be an instrument for slowing down the boom, why is he doing it in steps? If he is right, if there is a threat of inflation and if it is desirable to remove the sales tax in such a way as to do something about this situation, why does he not remove the entire 11 per cent on April 1, 1967? Obviously it would be a much better inducement for the manufacturer to postpone the purchase of machinery until next year if he stood to gain 11 per cent rather than 6 per cent by so doing.
If the minister's answer is that he wants to postpone purchases for two years I should like to ask him by what crystal ball was he able to ascertain that it was necessary to postpone these things for two years until April 1, 1968? If the minister reached the conclusion that it was socially desirable to remove the sales tax on production equipment and machinery of the kind described in the resolution, the sensible thing would have been to have removed it now in order to give manufacturers and producers the greatest incentive to improve productivity and thereby reduce the cost of production per unit. This is by far the best way of improving the economy. If, on the other hand, the minister has decided that he wishes to postpone this move in order to arrest the investment boom, then again he is taking mincing steps where decisive steps should have been taken.
I would indicate the same difference of philosophy in respect of the minister's refusal to remove the sales tax on building supplies. He said in his budget speech that he was not impressed by the need for this to be done. Yet, one of the effects of government policy has been to reduce housing starts.
I have before me a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of May 31. It is a report from the Canadian Press to the effect that there was a 26 per cent decline in housing construction starts in April compared with April, 1965, and a decline of 5.3 per cent in March compared with the same month a year earlier. This represents a serious decline in
June 7, 1966

housing construction. The first part of the story reads:
The housing boom continued to taper off In April with a 26 per cent decline in construction starts from a year earlier. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation reports. March starts declined 5.3 per cent from a year earlier.
The federal government's housing agency said that in the first four months of this year the number was down by almost seven per cent from the corresponding period last month.
Side by side there has been an increase in the cost of housing in all metropolitan centres of Canada. So we have a policy which the government claims is intended to reduce inflationary pressure but which in fact produces inflationary pressure as a result of the increased price of housing and the decline in housing production.
In case hon. members have not noticed it, may I draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in the consumer price index housing and household operations are given what the statisticians call a component weight of 32. In other words, they are given a 32 per cent weight in the total consumer price index structure. The government says it is taking these various measures in order to curb inflationary pressures and reduce prices. At the same time, the very programs it undertakes result in an increase in the cost of homes and of running homes. I earnestly suggest to the minister that in this field, as in the field of machinery and apparatus, he would serve the Canadian economy a great deal better if he would remove the sales tax and enable the construction of homes to increase as it should.
Finally, from my little knowledge of the effects of these economic forces, I have never yet known a plan designed to produce a certain result which did not at the same time have an opposite effect. The minister and his advisers must constantly figure out whether the advantages or the disadvantages would be greater. I maintain that the only way in which the government can achieve the results it wishes to achieve, presumably a slowing down of economic expansion, would be to slow it down in the right places by the encouragement of housing at the expense of costly shopfronts and stores, the encouragement of building homes for the aged and for the lower income groups at the expense of splendid but unnecessary bank buildings.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The only way they can achieve that kind of social weight in what they do is by seeing to
Excise Tax Act
it that socially desirable projects are continued and those less necessary are halted or slowed down. This should be done by direct measures, not by the indirect measures of reducing some taxes and spreading other reductions over two years and exerting moral persuation on people who do not listen to that kind of thing when the efficiency and profitability of their businesses are concerned. The government should take steps which will directly channel investment into the areas where we need investment and directly reduce investment in areas where such reduction or postponement does not produce undesirable social results.
Although I hope he will, I do not expect the minister to accept the general proposition I have made, but I do appeal to him, first, to reconsider the postponement of the elimination of the sales tax even on his own terms. He will get much better results if he does away with it altogether on April 1, 1967. At least there will then be some real inducement to postpone investment this year, and that may be enough. In fact, if he overdoes it he may induce things he does not want such as a contraction of some considerable proportion in our economic activity.
Second, I hope it is possible to persuade him to take another look at the removal of the sales tax on building supplies in order to stimulate the building of houses, in which field there is now a slowdown.
I was .in my constituency last week end, Mr. Chairman. I have, as I am sure other hon. members do, a centre to which those of my constituents who think I may be able to assist them can come. Among the many peo-ply who came to see me was a young couple with two children. The man is not unemployed. He is employed at a plant in Toronto which is unionized by one of the strongest unions in the country. He is provided with quite a considerable wage compared with other wages. He has a wage rate of over $2 an hour which compared with others is a pretty good rate, but this young couple cannot afford to pay the necessary rent to get decent housing.
They told me they could not find any housing, whether an apartment or a house, for less than $130 a month. This represents nearly one and two-thirds weeks of the man's earnings, much beyond what rental ought to be as a proportion of wages. Twenty per cent is the optimum figure, whereas he was going to have to pay something like 40 per cent or more of his wages.

When they came to see me they had been living in a place where they were paying $60 a month rent but, because of difficulty with the landlord with whom they had been sharing the home, at that point on a Saturday morning, with his wife and two children he was living in a home in which both the water and electricity had been cut off. His children were aged five and two, and their mother could not provide them with hot food. Because of the pressure on housing and the cost of homes even a man with $4,000 a year has difficulty obtaining decent housing.
The circumstances I have outlined should move the minister to take steps to control investment in order that the production of homes, and particularly of low income homes, is not cut down. Because of this 11 per cent tax on building materials and other measures taken by the government, the majority of the working people cannot afford decent accommodation. These are the observations I wanted to make at this stage in the hope that the minister may again look at the reduction of the sales tax in the areas I have indicated.

The Income Disability and Reinsurance Company of Canada was incorporated under the Corporations Act of Ontario by letters patent dated September 19, 1960, as a private company. At that time it was incorporated under the name "Income Insurance Company of Canada" as a private company, and by supplementary letters patent dated February 23, 1965 the name of the company was changed to Income Disability and Reinsurance Company of Canada and the company was converted to a public company.
This company was created for the purpose of selling accident and sickness insurance. Subsequently in December of 1963 a second company was incorporated by letters patent from the province of Ontario known as the Income Life Insurance Company of Canada and a bill in relation thereto was given second reading on May 24, 1966.
The original authorized capital was $1,500,000 divided into 15,000 shares of a par value of $100 each. The initial capital of approximately $300,000 was raised. The company was licensed by the province of Ontario in March, 1961, to transact the business of accident and sickness insurance. Subsequently the company was licensed to transact the same classes of insurance in the province of Manitoba in May, 1961, in Alberta and British Columbia in April of 1962 and in Saskatchewan in January, 1963.

We are considering four separate companies rather than the one referred to in the bill before us. The two companies concerned are somewhat like husband and wife in that they are almost indistinguishable in some of their relationships but distinguishable as individual

entities in others. The main distinction is the difference in the names. However, their directors are almost identically the same, their activities take place in the same fields, they have the same offices and employ the same people. Presumably they deal with the same people in selling and underwriting insurance.
We are not now simply dealing with the company referred to in Bill S-12 but rather, because of interconnections, with four companies, one of which was dealt with by the house a couple of weeks ago and the other two of which were incorporated by letters patent under the laws of the province of Ontario.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
It is interesting to note the scant attention that was given to these bills by the Senate. I should think that august body could engage itself in a little more intense consideration of a matter as important as this rather than just glossing over the surface and accepting the pronouncements of the sponsor of the bill in the other place that it was just a routine matter and really was not of much consequence.
We have in the bill some interesting individuals as the provisional directors: William Ewen Brunning who is an insurance executive from Burlington, Norman Graham James who is also an insurance executive from Burlington, Haliwell Soule, a trust executive, also of Burlington, Thomas Henry Baker, an investment executive from Toronto, William Richard Latimer, a solicitor from Toronto, Charles Alfred Read, a chartered accountant from Winnipeg, and Thomas Alexander Harriott, an insurance consultant from Winnipeg.
That is the extent of the provisional directors of a company which seeks the authority of this parliament to conduct its affairs throughout Canada, a company which already does business in the province of British Columbia but has not yet got around to finding a provisional director of the company from that particular province. I think this is a shortsighted policy because we have eminently qualified and capable people in British Columbia who would be a tremendous asset to Income Life Insurance Company of Canada and to Income Disability and Reinsurance Company of Canada. I wish the sponsor of the bill were in his place now so that I could direct some questions to him which he could answer in his closing remarks on second reading. My confrere from Tim-iskaming indicates that not only is the

sponsor of the bill not here, but there is not a quorum in the chamber to consider the proper conduct of the business of the house and the bill that is before us. However, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will not let that deter me from continuing my remarks.
As the sponsor of the bill announced, the company also does business in Alberta and-I am sure no one will disagree with this-in the province of Alberta there are likewise eminently qualified and capable persons who could become provisional or permanent directors of a company such as this. It seems rather a shame that this province, within which the company has undoubtedly done a tremendous amount of business, should have been left out in the selection of provisional directors.
We find therefore that the control of the company in so far as directors are concerned is contained within the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba and there is no one on the board of directors from any of the other provinces. Be that as it may, perhaps we should look further at the situation that the head office of the company will be in the city of Hamilton. It is not that there is anything that would detract from the operations of the company by having its head office in Hamilton or in the province of Ontario for that matter, but it is interesting that here again we have an addition to the control complex of the insurance world that exists in the southern Ontario area, out from which will extend the appendages of the company throughout Canada to extract insurance premiums and the like from whomsoever it is able to extract them.
It seems to me that in considering whether this company should be authorized to conduct its business in Canada we should look at the orientation of the company in terms of geographic location and effective control. As I have said, both are the insurance control complex that exists in southern Ontario surrounding and including the city of Toronto. It is proposed that the company's capital stock will be $5 million divided into shares of $5 each and the amount to be subscribed and fully paid before the general meeting for the election of directors is called shall be $1,750. This seems to me a rather small amount of money to be subscribed before the calling of the meeting to elect directors. It simply means that the provisional directors could very easily amongst themselves have already subscribed and paid the amount of $1,750 into
June 7, 1966

the company. They would thus be in a position to call the general meeting for the purpose of electing its permanent directors and in effect have themselves elected to the permanent directorship of the company. They would thus exclude, at least for the initial period, from the opportunity of becoming a director of this company anybody who may subscribe to the share capital of the company after the initial $1,750 has been subscribed and before the time the company actually gets into the business of selling insurance.
In order for the company to get to that stage it must have a subscription of at least $1,736,800 of its capital stock bona fide subscribed and at least $1,736,800 paid thereon. This means that all the stock subscribed for must be paid for before the company can get into business. This seems to me to be a kind of engineered arrangement whereby the sponsors or promoters of the company ensure that they become the permanent directors of the company, because they have incorporated in the bill a provision that the insignificant amount of $1,750, in terms of the $5 million capital structure of the company, is all that is required to be subscribed in order that the first meeting may be held.
It does not jibe with our concept of democracy for the promoters of a company of this sort to come to parliament and ask parliament to endorse a provision whereby they can establish a private law relating to their own election to the office of director of the company. What other reason can there be for keeping that figure at such a low level as $1,750?
I must apologize, Mr. Speaker. I have been making reference to the situation relating to a company and inadvertently I picked up Bill No. S-ll which we passed a couple of weeks ago. It is the companion bill to S-12 which is the one before us at the moment. This should be a decision of the Superintendent of Insurance whose duty it is to oversee the operations of insurance companies and to see that they meet the requirements of the public law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill I want to say at once, in spite of what I consider were rather frivolous interjections from the other side of the house, that the matter we have before us is in my view quite an important one. I think the gist of it is set forth in the opening part of the bill commonly referred to as the preamble in which certain private citizens of the country pray that their petition be enacted. It seems to me that the substance of the question we are debating is expressed in the phrase, "it is expedient to grant the prayer of the petition." The question we have to consider in relation to such bills as we now have before us is whether or not it is expedient that parliament should grant the particular petition set forth in Bill S-12. I think this perhaps sums up the principle of the bill we are considering.
In considering this bill my thoughts turn back to the subject matter of the discussion we were having in committee of the whole prior to our consideration private bills. We were discussing matters which seriously affect the economy and welfare of our country, namely, the taxation of production machinery, the sales tax and so on. We were discussing matters related to whether or not taxation should be imposed upon industry, upon production machinery and other things and whether or not this was an appropriate action to take in the light of our economic situation. I presume this was a serious matter which was considered important enough to be dealt with by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). On the other hand, this bill in my view asks us to do something which indirectly at least will authorize private individuals to impose upon citizens of Canada a form of taxation in many respects more onerous than the sales tax proposed by the Minister of Finance today, and when we think of the multiplicity of other bills seeking the authorization of private insurance companies we realize we are not considering proposals that will add to the production of the country. We are setting up machinery under which certain private individuals can garner an increasing measure of the surplus wealth of the country.
June 7, 1966

[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The more often we authorize new incorporations such as the one being requested in this bill, the greater the proportion of the savings of the people of Canada which will be drained off in useless, unproductive costs for overhead and operation. It is basically for this reason that I seriously question the advisability of granting the petition of the persons named in this bill. I think the time will come when there will be an increasing appreciation of the serious impact that this useless activity by an increasing number of citizens in our community is having on the total welfare of the nation. This is a matter which will require serious consideration by the members of this house.
When we were considering what was referred to as the companion bill, No. S-ll, in view of the close relationship of the personnel involved and the similarity of the title I made reference to the fact that Bill No. S-ll might as well be one to incorporate the Tweedledum company and this one might be referred to appropriately as the Tweedledee company. This may have been a somewhat jocular reference to the setting up of a sort of dual organization. Apparently these two firms are to operate as Siamese twins and rather than seeking an operation which would allow them to lead an independent existence they seem desirous of maintaining and strengthening the relationship.
It might be suggested that a more appropriate name than the Income Disability and Reinsurance Company, would be simply the redundant insurance company. I mean no discredit to the individuals who are involved in this application. As matters stand they are quite within their legal rights to make this kind of application. I am not suggesting they are any better or worse than thousands of other citizens of Canada who are interested in carrying on this kind of activity. But this is the parliament of Canada, Mr. Speaker. When we are called upon to consider whether certain actions on our part are expedient or not, our primary concern should be not for the individuals involved in a particular company but whether or not the action we are asked to endorse will be in the general interests of the people of Canada. My submission is that basically it is not. In other words, when it becomes obvious that this proliferation of insurance companies is being carried to the extreme we must begin to question seriously allowing this process to continue.
Private Bills
These are some of the questions with which the sponsor of the bill should attempt to deal when he asks us to give our assent to the passage of the bill. So far all I have heard from the sponsor-his introduction was no better and no worse than that of other sponsors-has been a reference to where the head office of the company would be and the names of some of the provisional directors of the company. I think it is time that members of the house who are prepared to sponsor bills of this sort should, in addition to giving us that type of factual information, be prepared to justify the bill they are sponsoring on the grounds of whether it is for the welfare of Canada. This is something they have not been doing. This is one reason I am raising these questions. I am not the member sponsoring this bill. I suggest there should be an onus on the sponsor of the bill to prove that the measure will be in the interests of the Canadian people and not merely something designed to provide a special privilege for a few particularly favoured individuals. These are the questions of principle that are involved.
It is not good enough in my submission for the sponsor of any private bill to be content to justify it on traditional, narrow grounds. In my opinion these bills ought to have a broader purpose than is apparent in this and other similar bills. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, that is the challenge I put to the sponsors of these bills. I say that on my part at least there is an increasing dissatisfaction with the placid approach we have been prepared to take to the passage of bills of this type.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
The hon. member for Skeena made reference to the fact that this bill had received rather casual treatment in the other place. I have not examined the records so I am not in a position personally to say whether or not his assessment of the situation is correct. What I am suggesting is that if we in this house are to be asked to consider whether it is expedient to allow this proliferation of insurance activity to continue with, as I have suggested, an increasing measure of basic economic inefficiency in providing insurance protection to individuals in various fields and with an increasing waste of the abilities and potential value to Canadian society of individuals absorbed in this sort of duplicating activity, then the sponsors of such bills in this house will have to provide more than

June 7, 1966
Private Bills
cursory justification for the proposals they sponsor.
This company, so the sponsor tells us, has been expanding its original operations in the province of Ontario to certain other provinces. When I was discussing Bill No. S-ll, which was put forward basically by the same people from the same part of Canada, I suggested that there was another aspect to the matter of companies of this kind which have apparently been engaged in business within a province and then come to parliament for a federal charter. It is the question of the division of jurisdiction and whether or not what we are being asked to do in effect is to circumvent some of the rights and powers of the provinces in the field of property and civil rights.
In my remarks on that question I referred to what I thought were the relevant sections of the British North America Act. I know that on that occasion the sponsor of the bill really did not have the opportunity to deal with these issues in connection with Bill No. S-ll, but perhaps before this bill carries he will give us his viewpoint on the question of our being asked to agree to federal incorporation which, if my understanding is correct, will swallow up the rights of the various provinces which have agreed to allow this company to conduct business therein.
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Skeena, the bill has some very interesting clauses and arrangements. The hon. member dealt with the question of the basic lack of democracy in the operations of companies of this kind. I am not sure I agree that that is restricted entirely to insurance companies. In my view there is a basic lack of democracy in the operations of many business enterprises in Canada under our present company laws.
My own feeling on the matter of insurance is this. If this company is not going to be operated under public auspices, where I believe it would be operated much more efficiently and economically, then it could much more properly be conducted under true co-operative principles where real democracy on the part of the shareholders prevails and policyholders rather than to a small group of individuals. However, that involves another area of debate and is perhaps not relevant to the question whether it is expedient that this insurance company be given a federal charter.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that that pretty well covers the questions in my mind at this time in relation to this bill. As the hon. member

for Skeena said, certain questions arise on some of the individual clauses which should have rather detailed discussion at the appropriate stage. But certainly in my view the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill should give us a much broader basis for his sponsorship than he has before the house is asked to assent its passage on second reading.

subtopic: INCOME DISABILITY AND REINSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that the sponsor of the bill has been making some notes but I would suggest to him that it is rather late for him to justify his position now. He was given the opportunity to do so and took advantage of it. Therefore I do not expect that he will redeem himself in relation to many of the matters which have been raised.
I am one of those who agree that if a member of this house sponsors a bill he must act very responsibly. By this bill the sponsor is really doing something for which there appears to be considerable support, that is, allowing the Superintendent of Insurance to make a decision whether the company is justified and whether the capitalization is sufficiently democratically oriented toward the special privileges which will be granted to the shareholders who, when the amount of $2,500 is raised, will be appointed directors of the company.
Many of these questions were asked when the hon. member was discussing these matters a week ago in connection with another bill. While I realize that the situation we are now discussing is better than the situation created by the sister bill in that the directors will have to raise another $750, this does seem a very small amount of money in return for the advantages which will obviously accrue to the directors and shareholders of this particular company.
Another problem which has been raised and which affects sponsors of this sort of bill-if you check the order paper, Mr. Speaker, you will find bills relating to a number of similar companies-is the question of the public good and the responsibility relating thereto. We are given to understand that this company originally applied to the Ontario government for a licence to operate in that province. By an act passed by the legislature of Ontario it was authorized to conduct business in that province.
I presume that the company has met certain requirements in relation to the operation of the insurance act of Ontario over the period of years it has been in business, but
June 7, 1966

the fact remains that it is now coming to the federal parliament for a federal charter. Therefore it behooves the house to give consideration to whether or not the company can assure members of parliament and the country in general that its operations will be for the good of the citizens of Canada and that there is a need for its operations.
In my opinion there is no justification for the statement that has been made that this company is a free enterprise operation which will operate in a competitive society. In my opinion there are no insurance, assurance or reinsurance companies which operate in a competitive manner at all. These companies have identical rates for identical risks, though the risks may vary somewhat and the type of insurance may vary. But the rates are identical for the same type of insurance in a given area. Therefore the system is not competitive; there is no free enterprise system operating. What we are really giving the insurance companies of Canada is a monopoly in the issuance of insurance. We have to be sure that there is some purpose involved and that special concessions are not being given to five or six people who want to enlarge the scope of their operations from the provincial to the federal field.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
We held a meeting with some officials of the house, including the house leader, with a view to arriving at some formula whereby such bills might be dealt with in another way. I know that in theory sponsors of these bills act without remuneration. In practice that often happens. Many times the sponsoring of these bills is a Joe-job handed out to various members and they therefore pay limited attention to it. I do not say that is true in this case because the company in question is in the riding of the hon. member sponsoring the bill. I presume he has an interest in it. The house is entitled to a better explanation about this company than the one he gave in committee where he indicated that he was aware of the good deeds performed by this insurance company and of its need to expand.
It would be surprising, Mr. Speaker, if we were to grant federal charters to insurance companies which have no interest in doing business in Canada. Doubts have been raised in my mind whether a federal charter might not be sought for reasons other than ostensibly reinsurance. It seems to me it should be the responsibility of the committee that is
Private Bills
charged with the administration of our financial institutions to give direction to this bill and to look into the things I have suggested.
It is very interesting to note that clause 8 (2) of the bill reads:
No agreement between the Company and the Provincial Company providing for such acquisition and assumption shall become effective until it has been submitted to and approved by the Treasury Board of Canada.
It is unfortunate that the sponsor of the bill did not explain this but so far as I can see that indicates that there are financial advantages to be gained under a federal charter which have no bearing to the issuing of insurance or reinsurance. Questions of tax may be involved. This company's business might be more advantageously conducted in the federal than in the provincial field. In this connection, some insurance companies are questioning the desirability of remaining in certain provincial fields. In at least two provinces there are indications that insurance companies there will have to serve the needs and interests of the people better or they will not remain under the control of their boards of directors and will be expropriated. I suggest that the expropriation of this company at $2,500 is not going to be an expensive proposition and should be undertaken.
I therefore reiterate that we are not giving serious enough consideration to the sponsoring of such bills because we lack knowledge about the companies and we lack explanations as to why many things are being sought. We are no longer willing to accept such things as a matter of course. Why should anyone come to parliament for a charter to issue insurance? It amounts to the same thing as asking for a charter to make money. Obviously the $2,500 needed with respect to this company will be found and also the $5 million in capital stock.
While we are reluctantly prepared to support this bill, as we did the other one, we should be prepared to rename this company when the bill returns, "Macaluso Income Disability and Reinsurance Company of Canada", because I think it would be more appropriate than caling it "Income Disability Company".

As the committee will notice there is one excise tax resolution and the resolution is divided into 18 paragraphs. I have been listening to the interesting remarks of members of the committee. Some of them were of a general character dealing with the principles which underlie these proposals. Others were more specific. I was waiting until I thought the committee had made their general observations before getting down to the text of the resolutions themselves.
It is difficult to know how best to deal with these matters. I myself have one amendment to propose and I will do this in due course; it arises out of representations which have been made since the budget was brought down. Perhaps I might deal now with one or two of the observations which have been made so far by members of the committee. First, as to the question raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West about the equipment used in the bituminous sands operation in Alberta. My understanding of the position is that this kind of equipment would probably all be of a character which would be defined as productive machinery while this specific item (i) deals with equipment used in natural gas or oil wells.
In other words, item (i) is an addition to a general description. I cannot vouch for this and it is difficult for me to give a legal opinion. My officials were puzzled by the representations from the hon. member because this point had never arisen before. But it is their belief, which I will confirm when the bills are before the house, that the kind of machinery which would be used in this bituminous sands operation would be covered in another part of the list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
As far as I know, the intention is not to be unduly restrictive. However, I will have the point examined in preparation for bringing the bill before the house.
A specific matter relating to drugs was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. In my budget address I made it clear that the government is prepared to remove the sales tax from drugs, should this course be recommended by the committee of this house which is concerned with the question of drugs and drug prices. The reason is that the government would like to be assured that the benefits of a reduction in tax would be passed on to the consumers; this is the only reason for our reluctance to move ahead now before the report of the committee has been presented.
As to the general question raised by the hon. member for York South-he is not here at the moment, but he will no doubt read this in Hansard when he gets an opportunity-regarding the economic effects of removing the sales tax on production machinery in one or two stages, we considered this matter very carefuly when we were preparing the budget proposals. The proposal to remove the sales tax from productive machinery in two stages was a deliberate decision in order to produce a specific effect upon the economy.
As I said in my budget speech, and as was said by the hon. member for Edmonton West, this is not a desirable kind of tax. It was imposed only because of the urgent need for revenue when we took office in 1963. I know that my former colleague, the hon. member for Davenport, agreed with me that the time had come to remove the tax which he never defended as being more than a necessary evil. He did not regard it as being a desirable form of tax. We were then faced with the question of how to remove it. If we had removed it immediately an unwanted impetus would have been given to expansion. Speaking of this, the hon. member for York South used words which I would never use.
