In order to explain the rewording of paragraphs 13 and 14 now before the committee it is necessary to say something about the reason for the amendments proposed by those paragraphs as originally drafted and as now presented in a revised form.
These two paragraphs as originally drafted, and as now revised, propose a change in the method of collecting the sales tax on furs. It is not proposed that there be any over-all increase in the amount of tax nor is any change to be made in the existing requirement that manufacturers of articles made from fur must pay sales tax when they sell the goods they manufacture. The purpose of the proposed change in the wording of the act is to provide greater certainty and efficiency in the collection of the sales tax on articles made from fur. In this industry many retail outlets carry out some manufacturing of fur
June 7, 1966

garments. It has proven difficult to ensure that sales tax is paid in all cases on the products of these manufacturing operations and this situation has been unfair to other manufacturers and unsatisfactory from the point of view of the treasury. What is proposed is to introduce a new procedure under which sales tax is collected at the stage where furs are dressed and dyed as well as at the time when fur garments are sold. In calculating the tax at the time fur garments are sold credit will be given for the tax paid at the dressing and dyeing stage.
As originally drafted, paragraphs 13 and 14 of the resolution proposed that dressers and dyers of furs would be responsible for the payment of sales tax on furs processed by them. This tax would have been payable by the dresser or dyer when he delivered furs to a manufacturer of fur garments. The manufacturer of fur garments would have been required to pay sales tax on the selling price of the garments and other articles made of fur manufactured by him at the time he sold these goods but in computing this tax he would have been allowed to take a deduction for the amount of tax already paid by the dresser and dyer on the furs he used in his manufacturing operations. That was the first proposal that I made and it was included in the resolutions tabled at the time of the budget.
Representations were made to the government by the dressers and dyers of furs that this arrangement would place them in very serious financial difficulties. Dressers and dyers of furs are not normally the owners of the furs they process. They only perform a service. It is traditional that the dressers and dyers extend long-term credits to the owners of the furs for the payment of the charges made for dressing and dyeing. Because of this arrangement the dressers and dyers would have been required to wait for many months for reimbursement from the owners of the furs for the sales tax paid by the dressers and dyers at the time they delivered the furs to their owners.
The only change of substance to be made in paragraphs 13 and 14 by the amendments now placed before the committee is to shift the liability to pay tax at the dressing and dyeing stage from the dressers and dyers to the person who takes delivery of processed furs from a dresser or dyer. That is, I hope, a simple explanation of what we are about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should begin our consideration of the Income Tax ^Resolution by saying to the committee that I shall have two amendments to propose to these resolutions arising out of representations that have been made following the presentation of the budget. Those amendments will relate to paragraphs 7 and 14.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we will now consider the principal part of the Budget resolutions, the one that has the greatest impact. I suppose most people look to it for some measure of glad tidings or for tidings of woe. This year I think in two senses it brought woe. First there was an increase in personal income tax-rendering ineffective that loudly hailed tax cut of last year, which was a pure election bait-and the other woe was to the economy. But the spelling of the word is whoa.
The editorial commentator in the Canadian Tax Journal of March-April, 1966, comment-
[The Deputy Chairman.]
ing on this particular aspect of the budget said:
Logically, since the measure was designed to dampen spending, last year's cut-which was designed to increase demand-might have been fully reversed-
One would think so-
-instead of increasing the tax cut for 40 per cent of the taxpayers.
Undoubtedly the increase in tax this year will hit some people harder. This will take a lot of computing. I suppose that if it is the intention of the government to restrain the economy, some sort of a tax should be imposed, but I am wondering whether the imposition of personal income tax is the right way to go about it. It certainly hits those people who have money to spend and it might deter them from spending money, depending upon how much the tax is increased. On the other hand, the person who pays no tax is not affected. All he is subject to is the burden of the increasing cost of living. This is fully understandable.
The minister, in his budget speech and certainly in his white papers, indicated he did not think the increase in the cost of living in 1966 should be smaller than it was in 1965. Therefore we are in for another rise in prices.
I was disappointed in certain aspects of the budget speech. First of all I had hoped that the minister would have realized the impropriety of the ministerial discretionary provisions which were introduced in 1963 with regard to associated companies. A great deal of objection was voiced both in and out of the house-as a matter of fact there was a great deal of objection from certain members supporting the present minister-when his predecessor introduced these discretionary powers. I find them completely repugnant and I sincerely regret that the minister did not remove them from the act.
There is one thing however in which we can perhaps rejoice and that is in the fact that the minister has not introduced the capital gains tax. If he has given a look to the initial drafts of the Carter Commission report he may or may not have seen that some indication was given there to the necessity of introducing a capital gains tax into Canada's tax structure. Personally, I do not think we should do so since we are trying to encourage development capital in this country. This is what the minister and his predecessors have been endeavouring to do at all times, to encourage equity investment. The
June 7, 1966

introduction of a capital gains tax would be an absolute deterrent to equity investment.
I find it rather odd that my friends to the left of us in the house on the one hand advocate a capital gains tax and on the other hand want Canadians to invest more in the development of our own resources. The two propositions are quite incompatible. Some countries have considered a capital gains tax only after they have achieved a mature investment state, and even in those cases I am sure that in essence a capital gains tax, under today's economic structure is improper. If there is a capital gains tax, surely there must be an allowance for capital losses. We never hear about them. They are always to be taken as part of the price of living. Rather, they go after the gains. This is something that must be taken to be quite improper, something that will stultify all initiative and activity. In my opinion, unless you are prepared to make a concession on the losses, then do not talk about taxing gains.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
One other matter that I do find regrettable in this income tax resolution is the element of retroactivity. One need not belabour the undersirability of having retroactive features in any taxing statutes. However, there is that feature in this Budget. It deals with the restriction now placed on certain stock options. I must say that there have been many representations made, both by the financial press and elsewhere, and I should like to read some excerpts from a document written by a business concern in this country where the employees do have stock options. This article is written from the point of view of equity and what happens as a result of the provisions which are contained in subparagraph (7) of the resolution.
The amendment to section 85A of the Income Tax Act proposed in the Budget speech of March 29 has the following effect: As the act stands at present, an employee may elect to pay a tax on benefits received from the employee stock option plan at his average tax rate for the previous three years, less 20 per cent of the benefits. The 20 per cent reduction, which at present is not limited, would now be limited to $200. I would say that in most cases this limitation results in a very substantial extra tax burden on the employee.
Now, this provision has no bearing on the restraining of the expansion or the limiting of the inflation which seems to be the main theme of the Budget. If it is related to the
Income Tax Act
closing of a loophole, then it is difficult to imagine what abuses have taken place or could take place under an employee stock option plan. After all, the granting of stock options in so far as public companies are concerned is rigidly policed by the stock exchanges in order to guard against any abuses. Now, why has this provision been made retroactive?
As I said, the 20 per cent deduction of benefit has been limited to $200, making the stock option a relatively costly form of remuneration. The changes, apparently, will not apply to options granted before the beginning of 1965 and exercised before the end of 1966, and the result is to trap a number of situations which cannot meet this exemption requirement. I am sure there are many employees, of one category or another, who undertook certain employment or who committed themselves on the basis of the tax law as it was. Now, along in the middle of the game, a change is made. So far, the minister has not been able to explain or has not explained why the change was made. What was the nature of the abuse, if there was one? I feel we clearly have to have an explanation. As will be seen the minister, in order to justify this income tax amendment, must overcome the objection to retroactivity, which is always a repugnant feature in any taxation statute.
I should like to say that I am pleased to see important efforts have been made to regularize charitable organizations, so that one can readily establish the continuing charitable nature of any organization which is prepared to apply initially to the Minister of National Revenue for status, and be able to grant a receipt which is good for income tax deduction purposes. However, I do believe there will be some administrative difficulty. This has not been disclosed in the resolution, but with regard to religious bodies is it the intention to have every parish, every church, which would normally be entitled, under section 62 I believe of the act, to grant a charitable donation receipt, register and file its report? Will this be done, for instance, through the presbytery, through the diocese or the archdiocese, so that there will be one regional authority in regard to the church? Will the various religious bodies certify to the Minister of National Revenue that such and such a parish is in good standing and has the authorized person to issue charitable donations receipts? Otherwise, there is going to be

June 7, 1966
Income Tax Act
a tremendous staff required by the Department of National Revenue to examine and file these annual statements called for by this amendment.
One feature with regard to charitable donations which I find neglected in this year's budget and which I feel would have merited a great deal of support in the house and in the country, concerns donations in excess of the statutory limit, provided those donations are made to a recognized educational institution. This would encourage endowments to university foundations. I feel we could do a great deal more than we have done. I spoke about this during the Budget debate. There are some things that have been done at the University of British Columbia during the past year or two, where tremendous gifts have been made to the university by people who have been able to amass a jolly good share of this world's goods, and who are putting it to good public use. I think we should be in a position to encourage this type of thing.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
The last matter about which I want to speak, because there will be a number of others who will want to do so, concerns the refundable levy. This has really been called in some quarters a corporation tax loan. Because that is all it is. The minister says that corporations and certain types of trusts shall, if their income exceeds $30,000 a year, pay a 5 per cent levy on the excess over that income, which may be refundable with interest up to some period not exceeding 18 months. It is a forced loan, and I know that many concerns will be caught. Some concerns because of their cash position, will have to borrow the money in order to pay this tax. It will be interesting to know whether they will be able to claim as a business expense the interest on the money which they have to borrow in order to pay the so-called corporate tax loan.
On the other hand, the 5 per cent interest which the crown will pay on the refund I am sure will be charged as taxable income. So I trust the interest on the money borrowed to pay this tax should be charged as an expense. I seem to recall that in the past there were some monarchs who incurred a great deal of censure when they forced their subjects to make loans to the crown. History today finds their conduct rather reprehensible.

Here the government is doing the same sort of thing; they are forcing some of our subjects to make loans. I do not know what is the government's justification for telling these people that it is going to force them to pay this money; that they will be paid less than the going rate of interest on the money; and that they will have to pay tax on this interest. To me this is not justifiable.
I do not know how this is going to help the economy. As the Canadian Tax Journal forecasts, is something of the nature of $145 million to be removed from the economy? I would have thought that if the minister had been able to exercise the degree of influence with his provincial counterparts he would have done far more good by having them reduce the totality of the provincial budgets by $145 million. The economy would have benefited far more than by this roundabout method of going after corporate business. I am not too sure that corporate business in this country should be loaded down with more and more burdens. There is such a thing as killing the goose that lays the golden egg; or perhaps I can use another simile- knocking the milk cow on the head.
The economy of Canada must continue to retain a viable form. It must produce economic activity. It must produce income or revenue if the government is anticipating that the economy will be able to pay its share of the expense of administering the country, provide for the many government programs, as well as provide for an expansion of the economy. It always seems that whenever the economy is expanding, public authority wants a bigger and bigger slice of the expansion. I think that is evident. When I say "public authority" I refer to the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government. That is the public authority which is going after a bigger and bigger portion of the economic expansion, a manoeuvre which, of course, is self-defeating.
Somehow or other we have to bend our energies toward finding some other solution. In this regard I trust we will derive some help from the report of the Carter Commission. I know that all the Minister of National Revenue wants is a nice straightforward and simple system whereby he can collect his taxes. We know that he is not the one who sets the budget: The Minister of Finance does that, though from the way the Minister of National Revenue is looking at the present time he might have had a few suggestions to make with regard to the present budget.
June 7, 1966

I know many other members of the committee wish to make some remarks at this stage. The exact detail of this resolution and of the legislation will be better studied in committee of the whole when the bill is before us.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I very briefly and in a rather elementary way indicate the framework of the remarks I wish to make. First of all I want to ask, what are the purposes which a fiscal system ought to serve? Unless one has those purposes in mind it seems to me he goes in a routine way from one problem to another, whether it be a budgetary or any other type of problem. What purposes should a fiscal system serve in addition to raising revenues to meet the necessary expenditures?
I suggest there are two major purposes which are equally important for the economy, for the people who make the economy function and for whom the economy exists. Some spokesmen I listen to are economists and some are politicians. Sometimes they are both, or from other groups. But many of them talk about the economy as if there were something useful in the economy itself aside from the people the economy has to serve. It is as if you are making something function just because there is some virtue in making it function per se. I see no virtue in making the economy function, other than that it be made to function for the welfare of the people not only in this country but in other countries as well.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, from that point of view I suggest that the tax system ought to have two purposes in mind; and I am not saying that either one is more important than the other. The first is to use the fiscal system as a means of income redistribution. If there is anything true about our present society it is that inequality of income persists, and indeed grows greater rather than smaller, as our wealth increases. That is the first purpose that a fiscal system should serve. Second, it ought to serve the purpose of being one of the tools by which the economy is kept functioning at full or as near full capacity as possible.
It seems to me that what has happened is that the minister and those around him have gone about as far as John Maynard Keynes -perhaps not quite as far-and have stopped there. I suggest that it is not enough today to deal with rates of investment in the total, global sense, but that in modern societies you must be much more selective about
Income Tax Act
your channels and direction of investment, as well as your global rate of investment. When therefore the Minister of Finance sets out in a time of expansion, because he fears inflation, to reduce the total purchasing power in society he takes a step that is bound to discriminate against those who can suffer discrimination least. That is what this budget does.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I start therefore with a question so simple that the economists, certainly under the guidance of the Minister of Finance, seem to have overlooked it. The simple question is: How much does it cost for a family consisting of a mother, father and two children to live, not luxuriously, but relatively decently? We find that the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto produced a guide to family budgeting some time ago for such a family. Their budget was designed to provide for a level of living sufficiently above the subsist-ance survival level as to be consistent with the maintenance of good health and a sense of self respect, and yet considerably below any level of living that might be called luxurious. In another part of the introduction to this budget the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto states that in the budget some commonplace wants are included that are so important to the social and emotional well-being of families that they rank with necessities.
This is the kind of budget I have in mind, providing for decent yet not luxurious living for a mother, father and two children, one 13 and one nine. The budget provides only $112 a month for food, $38 a month for clothing for all four; 75 cents a month for school needs; $4.55 a month for life insurance; and $115 a month for rent, heat, water, electricity and gas, all inclusive.
This budget provides for no more than any family in Canada ought to have as a minimum. It shows the absolute floor to income of a family of this size, in order for that family to live decently. Bringing that budget up to date, what would it cost a family to live decently in April, 1966? You have a requirement, according to the budget for that family, of $389.49 per month, or $4,673.88 per year. That, according to an authority that is as impartial as may be is the minimum required for a family of four to live in relative self-respect.
What does that mean? It means, I suggest, that the Minister of Finance in looking at this

June 7, 1966
Income Tax Act
budget should, as I urge, come to the conclusion that any family of four persons that makes no more than $4,000 a year ought not to have to pay income tax at all.
Instead, what does the Minister of Finance do? He plays around with bits and pieces of window dressing. He restores the income tax that was cut last year. He ostensibly changes the percentage of the cut from 10 per cent to 20 per cent, and then imposes a ceiling of $20 on it. The result, as will be found on page 3384 of Hansard for March 29, 1966, is that the married taxpayer with two dependant children eligible for family allowances has to pay on the $4,000 income, if he makes it, $97 in 1966 instead of the $100 which he paid in 1965, and presumably that would be $95 in a total year, with respect to, say, 1967, instead of the $100 he paid in 1965.
This family which already, according to the budget of the Social Planning Council for Metropolitan Toronto has an income which is $700 below that necessary for a relatively reasonable standard of life, still has to pay $95 in income tax. That is not all. That is why we of the New Democratic Party believe that the minister's budget this year-and I am putting this strongly and deliberately-takes no cognizance of the needs of the lower income groups of this country. Not only does the family I have referred to have to pay $97 in taxes this year and $95 in income tax next year but, in addition, as a result of the Canada Pension Plan the head of a family has to contribute to that plan, if my calculations are correct, some $61 a year, or 1.8 per cent of $3,400. The head of the family therefore this year has to pay $61 that he did not have to pay last year. In addition, the head of the family must pay an additional $52 old age security tax. On top of that, in most provinces he will have to pay an additional $30 in provincial taxes. This means that the family which already is $700 below the minimum income level required for living with reasonable self respect has to pay $210 roughly in federal taxes of one kind or another, plus $30 in provincial income taxes, plus sales tax for various things such as drugs, which the minister has refused to exempt.
We say consciously and deliberately knowing precisely what we say; the minister says consciously and deliberately knowing exactly what he is doing, that the family of four, already in receipt of a gross income below what it ought to have, will have its purchasing power still further reduced in order to make sure that the economy keeps going.

That, in my submission, ignores the basic purpose of a fiscal system, which has to do with the redistribution of income, in order to help those at the lower levels of income to make some kind of half decent living.
I therefore urge the minister even at this late date to consider rearranging the tax structure so that below a certain level of income-and $4,000 for a family of four is the level I have based my submissions on-income should not be taxable at all. I want to make clear that I am not proposing that the exemptions be raised. If you raise the exemptions that would make a difference to those in the higher income brackets to a much greater extent than to those in the lower income brackets.
I am proposing a reconstruction of the total income tax rate structure so that families consisting of a father, mother and two children of, say, six and seven and earning only $4,000 a year do not have to pay any income tax. That family will still be paying toward the Old Age Security Act, and toward the Canada Pension Plan. It will be making many other contributions, as a result of which its income will not be a net income, but will be gross, before deductions.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Parliament should say to this family: We will take no more money from you. This would mean that the minister would have to find his revenue elsewhere; he would have to increase the taxes which those of us who make the salaries we make as members of this parliament, perhaps plus added income as well, would have to pay, and that is precisely what, morally and socially, the income tax system ought to accomplish. It should give those at the bottom of the ladder an opportunity to live in decency. If this means that those of us who are at the middle or top of the ladder must pay more, then we should pay more.
I was not particularly moved by the plea of the hon. member for Edmonton West, that there should not be a capital gains tax because it would lead to a drying up of investment. People said this about the corporations tax when it was first introduced. They said it would kill initiative, destroy business sense, murder private enterprise and ensure that the economy would come to a halt. But since the corporations tax was introduced our economy has grown by leaps and bounds.
The fact that the corporations have had to pay income tax on their profits has not prevented them from showing phenomenal
June 7, 1966

increases in the rate of profit every year for the last few years. The same thing would happen, I am sure, if there were a capital gains tax.
If the minister, being moved as he ought to be by humane considerations, and as he is capable of being by virtue of his character, were to remove the tax from people receiving small incomes and ask where he was to find the money to replace this revenue, my answer would be: You will find it in the capital gains tax and in the incomes of those who make gains, sometimes large and sometimes small, without doing anything except take the risk of investment. I am not saying that this risk should not be recompensed. It certainly should be. But there is no reason why earnings of this kind should be free of tax, whereas every other type of earning is taxable.
My learned friend, the hon. member for Edmonton West, asks: What about compensation for losses? If he would put the question differently I would have no quarrel with him. He is saying that in some areas one makes gains, and in other areas losses, and that therefore the losses should be taken into consideration.
I would have no objection to a capital gains tax scheme which provided for the averaging of returns over a period greater than one year. Whether the period should be two, three or five years, I would not say; that is an administrative detail with which we are not concerned at this point. But it is certainly possible to devise a capital gains tax system which would make allowances for the year in which there were losses.
I cannot refrain from drawing attention to the distinction between the way the minister addresses himself to the lower income groups in our society and the way he addresses himself to those companies for which the hon. member for Edmonton West, if he will excuse me for putting it this way, wept so charmingly some minutes ago.

No, not copiously. It was like the minister's attempt to control the economy: It was moderate weeping. The hon. member said it was a terrible thing to impose a refundable income tax on these people, even though it was to be repaid with interest at 5 per cent. It amounts to a forced loan, says he. I do not care what he calls it. Since there is, I believe, a floor of $30,000 under profits before the refundable income tax 23033-387
Income Tax Act
provision applies, I do not think we should weep copiously or even moderately for these corporations.
But look at the way we treat another group in our community. We say to the $4,000 a year man, who has'a family of two children, that in addition to the contribution he must make to the old age pension plan amounting to $61 a year, and in addition to the $52 he has to pay in old age security tax, he will still have to pay a further $97, or about $2 a week-and he will not get it back, with or without interest. "Too bad", says the Minister of Finance. "But because I realize the difficulty of your situation I will be generous: Last year you had to pay $100 in tax, this year you'll have to pay only $97. And I ask you to be grateful to me for this indication of my generosity." Three bucks a year.
What a difference of approach when it comes to the corporations. Even when he takes the slight step of imposing a refundable tax of only 5 per cent, as a faint-hearted measure to control the rate of expansion in the economy the minister promises to return it to them after 18 months, to do with as they will, plus 5 per cent interest on top. I submit this is characteristic of the kind of society we have built and the kind of social attitudes which motivate us in this nation. This is the protest I am bound to make.
It is to be noted that neither the former minister of finance in 1965 nor the present Minister of Finance has made any change in the income tax structure. I summarize what I have said by making an appeal to the minister to reconstruct the income tax system altogether, not necessarily in terms in which the Carter Commission might propose, but in the simple terms whereby those earning less than a certain amount will not be taxed at all.
I repeat: Do not increase the exemptions, but reconstruct the tables so that a family with two children does not need to pay any taxes out of an income of $4,000. Should the income be less than $4,000 a year, the family should certainly pay no taxes. Even under the new scheme a man with $3,500 a year would have to pay $53 a year in taxes. I submit that such a family with two dependant children, already $1,200 below the minimum for self-respecting living, cannot afford the dollar a week we propose to take from it in income tax. I urge the minister to give this whole question his consideration.

June 7, 1966
Income Tax Act
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I turn now to the refundable tax. My hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and I made reference to this in our speeches on the budget, and I wish to do so again. It is a great pity that the minister did not have the courage to introduce this very useful planning lever in a meaningful way once he started. He has taken a weak step in the direction of some form of investment planning. It is an inadequate step. It will not do anything because the amount he is going to take out of the investment total is so very low that it will have no effect at all.
The fact is that there is a great deal in the investment reserve idea. I do not have to tell the minister about the Swedish plan. Under it a carrot rather than a stick is used. A corporation may put into the investment reserve some 40 per cent of its total undistributed profits, and this amount remains in the reserve with the corporation not having to pay taxes on it. This is the carrot, and a very large carrot.
The reserve is held in government hands, and the corporation is given two alternatives. Either it can withdraw the money when it desires to do so, in which case it pays the income tax at that time, or it can leave the money in the reserve until the government decides that the investment needs of the country require it, in which case the corporation is given certain remissions, the details of which frankly I cannot remember. In this way the government can undertake real planning.
But the major part of the Swedish plan which I commend to the minister is that when the government releases the funds, it says where they are to be invested, where a factory or whatever it is is to be built. In that way you have a useful area development plan, as well as a plan that helps keep the economy as a whole going.
I cannot sufficiently emphasize, and I hope I am not too far from right in economic terms, that we are past the stage when we should consider the economy globally every time we take some step. It is necessary for us to consider the various areas of the economy and how they are each affected. The great value of the Swedish plan is that you have a relatively large reserve available to the government for investment. I think it is the Bank of Sweden and the Swedish Labour Market Board which indicate not only when but where the money is to go, in what kind of industry and in what area of the country.

This is the kind of plan which in the view of the New Democratic Party is absolutely minimal under the present circumstances of the complex society in which we live, and it is essential for us to take steps for such planning. The minister looked at that, but instead of adopting the Swedish plan, or some version of it that would give him a real planning lever, he took this miniscule, mincing step of the 5 per cent refundable tax which will accomplish nothing, and which will help those who need help least in the business world.
I suggest that the large corporations, many of which are subsidiaries of American parent companies, will easily replace the amount of the 5 per cent refundable tax from the treasuries of their parent companies. Others will be able to borrow from the money market, even if the interest rate is a little higher. Further, if they take that 5 per cent from their American parent companies, that will be a further injection of U.S. funds which may be something that the minister wants.
Those who will be hurt by this 5 per cent refundable tax are the smaller companies with profits of more than $30,000, with no parent companies to replenish what the minister has taken from them, nor can they afford to go to the money market where interest rates are relatively high.
This is constantly the way in which we do our fiscal work in this country. We take a step which in effect means no harm at all to those who can best afford to be hurt, and which does most harm to those who can least afford to be hurt.
I could deal with a good many other points which are in this income tax resolution but I have spoken long enough and have tried to touch upon the two points that most concern us in the New Democratic Party. I conclude by saying that we will not have a fiscal system that meets the needs of a modern society unless we have the courage to use it effectively and conscientiously for the redistribution of income. We should have the courage to use it to enable the lower income groups to have the highest standards they can in the circumstances of their income, by not taking any income tax from them, and we should have the courage to use it as part of a plan to make sure not only that the economy as a whole expands but, more importantly, that every area in the economy benefits from that expansion.
June 7, 1966

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of the consideration of those items to say a few words about the Income Tax Act. In the first place, I think it would be advisable to mention to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) that this is probably one of the last years he will be managing or controlling direct taxes collected in the province of Quebec.
Indeed, we all know that not only before-and this can indicate the seriousness of the statement-but especially since his coming to power, the new Quebec premier has deemed advisable to state that from now on Quebec will ask and demand 100 per cent of direct taxes collected in the province, including personal and corporation income taxes.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the new Quebec premier was right in making that request and we admire him for it because he is trying to obtain what belongs to Quebec, under the British North America Act and our constitution, that is all direct taxes collected within the province.

Mr. Chairman, the second point I want to discuss tonight deals with the 10 per cent reduction of personal income tax granted by the minister's predecessor. I start out by saying that I am against this tax, on principle, because I think it is just one more nuisance for business to contend with and should not have been imposed. I would hope the minister will take into consideration the various representations that have been made to him in this regard, will see fit to reconsider this tax, and will take it off before it does any harm.
I have only to point out that the predecessor of the Minister of Finance in his first and succeeding budgets made numerous proposals and many of those proposals, because of the

June 7, 1966
Income Tax Act
cry that was raised in the house and by business generally throughout Canada were taken off or modified. To point up my argument I have only to remind the minister of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production equipment. Such a howl was raised at the time this tax was imposed that I believe the then minister would have liked to withdraw it. The howl in connection with this tax came from business in this country and the arguments used were good ones. The argument was that it would hamper business in Canada, increase the costs, would not bring in any revenues and would hamper Canada in her trade throughout the world. I believe it would have been withdrawn right away had the previous minister of finance not made so many withdrawals that one more would have probably pulled the plug out from the bottom of the boat and let him sink. What he did instead was to impose it in three stages.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The one thing that we have inherited from the last budget is the statement made by the minister that he will gradually withdraw the tax on building materials. The reason I pointed this out is that I believe the refundable tax, this levy against corporations, will have a very harmful effect indeed. The minister said in his budget speech:
The other temporary measure Is designed to divert and immobilize temporarily a modest portion of the flow of funds that is the chief source of finance for the increasing capital expenditure of businesses.
Mr. Chairman, I will ask the minister a question. Who decides whether a particular business should make or should not make further capital expenditures? If it is necessary for a business to make capital expenditures, then surely it is up to the business itself to decide. The government should not put its foot down on normal capital expansion.
The minister said there is a purpose behind this, and that he is doing it so as to divert capital from the market. He may be right in certain things, but I think that in this case no benefit whatsoever is derived from this withholding tax. If money for capital expenditures is withheld from a business for a period of one and a half to three years, then it will have to get its money elsewhere. In his Budget speech the minister said that this will be done at no expense to business, and that he is even going to pay them 5 per cent. I would like to see any corporation in Canada

trying to borrow money on the open market at anywhere near 5 per cent. I say that if capital expenditure must be made by a corporation, then there is no question at all that it will cost it more than 5 per cent.
One of the avowed intentions of this government, and I believe of previous governments as well, has been to let Canadians use their own capital to develop their country. In fact, only a few days ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated to the Canadian Manufacturers Association that Canadians should use their own capital to develop their country, that they should be masters in their own house. He also said that we welcome foreign capital because we cannot do without it. That is all the more reason why every effort should be made to use all the money that we can.
Where will the funds come from? There is only one answer. If this government will put this money in the fund, withhold it and then pay it back after one and a half to three years, then that money will have to come from outside Canada. This is just one more factor in the imbalance of payments which the minister says we always have in boom times, because capital has to flow in from foreign sources. He also stressed this in his budget speech. Why then withhold this Canadian capital and not use it for capital expenditures, while at the same time allowing corporations to borrow it from foreign sources? This will certainly increase our trade imbalance which has already reached the danger point. For the life of me I cannot see why the minister should take away this money from the corporations. Mind you, he does not steal it-it is called a tax-but he takes it away and says it will be deferred for a period of possibly 18 months. However, it has been my experience that once a tax is imposed, it remains, and will probably be kept forever. According to the budget resolution, the corporations will be paying a modest tax for three years. In fact I do not think it is modest. I wonder how much it will grow.
This money will be taken off the market for three years, and if the tax continues it will never be repaid because of the nature of this revolving fund. No corporation will see any of the moneys which they have paid in. They will only receive 5 per cent on it, and if they need capital they will have to borrow it at more than 5 per cent.
We have heard a lot about the Canada development fund. This is a great fund which is to be established to help Canadian industry
June 7, 1966

to develop. Why not let our Canadian industrialists and manufacturers do their own developing? Why take away the money with one hand, and hold it out with the other? I do not believe anything much will come from the Canada development fund. However, even if something comes of it, I say to you beware, because the money that is taken away from you at 5 per cent interest will be loaned to you under another name, and you will be charged considerably in excess of 5 per cent, cent.
I believe I have demonstrated that this special refundable tax put forward under section 15 of the budget resolution will inevitably create a chain reaction which can only harm Canada. The government in loco parentis says to business "We are doing it in your best interest", on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.
I believe this tax is wrong and I believe it is harmful to the economy of Canada. I believe it makes this large pool of money sterile for business and development purposes. It is all very well for the minister to say we will have a nice reserve fund to which we can look forward. I say that if this tax is imposed it will remain, because such is the history of taxes. speechtext:
I should like to make a brief statement about paragraph 2 of the income tax resolution, particularly to explain what is planned as regards the registration of charitable organizations. My department has been concerned for some time about the abuses which have developed in the matter of exaggerated receipts for which charitable donation deductions were claimed, a situation with which all hon. members are well acquainted.
I should like to point out to hon. members that where a charitable donation is claimed that should not be claimed, in the case of an individual a deduction of 13.5 per cent and up to 80 per cent is being made, and in the case of a corporation a deduction of 21 per cent or 50 per cent is being made.
Another source of concern is the possibility that organizations which once had been given formal approval could subsequently change the nature of their activities so that they no longer qualify. There is also the question of those organizations whose names could lead to the ready acceptance of their receipts, when in fact those bodies might not qualify as proper charitable organizations. The officials of my department have done excellent work to cope with the many problems engendered by the situation. They have, however, been handicapped in their efforts by the lack of provisions for regulatory control in the income tax law.
The Auditor General recognized this and, in his report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1965, recommended that consideration should be given to the setting up of adequate controls over the many charitable organizations now recognized. It is therefore being proposed that the necessary amendments to the Income Tax Act be introduced to provide for the required controls. Paragraph (a) of the resolution is intended to bring in more clear cut and specific provisions in respect of gifts to charitable organizations in Canada. Paragraph (b) is to permit the deduction of donations to certain specified classes of charitable organizations outside of Canada. It should be noted that neither of these provisions will affect the existing provision whereby a taxpayer may deduct up to $100 for charitable contributions and medical expenses without submitting receipts.

In accordance with paragraph (a) of the resolution, it is proposed that all charitable organizations in Canada will be required to register and to file annual returns of information if donations to them are to be permitted as deductions from income. Each individual organization, whether it is a branch, section, or other division of a greater organization, will have to register and file an annual return of information if it receives donations on its own behalf and wishes to have its receipts qualify for deduction. Receipts will still have to be filed as evidence of payment of the amount given, but the proposal is that they be in a form which meets certain requirements. Regulations will be published for the guidance of those concerned.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The prescribed form of application for registration will be designed to obtain the particulars required to permit an intelligent assessment of the validity of the request for approval. There is already a form known as T511, which has been used in the past by organizations voluntarily seeking approval for income tax purposes. While a new form will be designed for the purposes of the new proposal, it will probably be very similar to the existing one. It is the intention to make these new forms available as soon as the proposed legislation is passed so that the work of registration can commence immediately. It would be my hope that the great bulk of registrations could be completed before the beginning of next year, at which time the proposals, if passed, will become effective. That is, they will become effective on January 1, 1967.
It is felt that every well-managed charity, congregation, parish, or like body can readily produce some kind of financial statement each year. Indeed most, if not all of them, now prepare such statements either for their own good management, for distribution to their members, or even for publication. The annual return of information to be prescribed will include the production of a statement which will give the revenue from different sources and some details of the operating and functional disbursements to show how the money was spent, and determine the nature and the extent of the activities carried on by the organization.
It is thought that a copy of the financial statements now prepared by the organizations concerned will, in the majority of cases, meet the requirements. The intention is to design
June 7, 1966

the annual return of information form in such a way as to include some questions that can readily be answered yes or no, questions that will, as well as provide some indication of the continued compliance with the requirements, serve as guide lines to the organizations themselves.
As to receipts, it is proposed that they should preferably be prenumbered and that, definitely, duplicate copies should be retained. In addition, they should, with the name of the organization, bear the statement that the organization has been registered as a Canadian charitable organization, and quote the registration number. The intention is that, commencing with the 1967 taxation year, any claims for charitable donations which are not supported by such a receipt will be disallowed.
Effective control is not possible without judicious examination of the affairs of the organizations recognized and some examination of the records. It is not proposed that all charitable organizations will be examined or audited each year. But a reasonable number should be looked at each year to test the efficacy of the system and, certainly, those which give indication that their operations should be examined further will be investigated.
In brief, Mr. Chairman, I am indicating that what we are trying to do is to find some system of tying in the number of receipts issued by a charitable organization with the total annual receipts which they report in their financial statement to the people contributing to the organization.
To carry out the implementation of the new provisions, my department proposes to organize a new unit to be known as the charitable organizations section, in the assessments branch of the taxation division. The official in charge of this section would be called the registrar-examiner of charitable organizations. The functions of the section would be to receive and review all applications for registration, keep adequate records of the registrations, receive and examine the prescribed information returns filed yearly, direct the program of audit and investigation to be carried out by the assessing staff at the district offices, develop the forms required and the regulations necessary, recommend such changes or amendments as might become advisable, and generally carry out the new provisions of the law.
I should like to indicate to all hon. members that in moving toward a little more 23033-388
Income Tax Act
control over the use of receipts for charitable donations in Canada it is not the intention of the government or of my department to disallow any legitimate charitable donations to organizations who are approved as charities and who carry out charitable purposes in this country. Rather this is a move toward a system of control whereby people may not abuse the right of being a charitable organization to the detriment of all other taxpayers in Canada, and thus force those taxpayers to pay more tax to make up for the advantage taken of this system by people who should not do so.

I should also like to speak for a moment about the 5 per cent refundable tax by which this government is attempting to discourage industry from increasing its facilities to increase production. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in the examination of his estimates in committee the other day, was asked by myself why it was that the rate of increase in export sales has fallen oft very considerably in the last year as compared with the year before, he said that it was largely because Canadian industry could not produce enough to make available the required volume of goods for export. He said that our demands in Canada have increased very considerably, and that the productive capacity of industry in this country was taxed almost to the full, and there was very little left over for the export market.
What we must obviously do, therefore, is to increase our productive capacity in this country so that we can fill the orders which are waiting to be filled by Canadian goods in the export market. If those orders are not filled by Canada, they will be filled by someone else, as they obviously are being filled today, and will be filled in the future. If we do not fill them, our customers will become satisfied with the goods they are receiving from other
June 7, 1966

countries, and the sales we ought to be making will be lost in the future, with a very real loss to Canadian production and to the Canadian standard of living.
It is obvious, Mr. Chairman, that this country must produce more. But if we are to increase production we must first of all increase the means of increasing production. That needs two things, Mr. Chairman. First of all it needs more capital, and second, it needs more skilled workers, which are in such short supply today. It is obvious that the Minister of Finance can make a very real contribution in this regard. He and the government can ease the tight money policy that has been reducing the amount of money available to industry to expand production. Also, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration can attract more skilled workers to this country by making it so attractive for them to come here from other industrial countries that they literally cannot afford not to come. That is the program followed by industry, as we all know. When industry is expanding and needs certain key personnel, it goes out and literally lures them away from its competitors.
If we want more skilled workers, we must either greatly increase our means of training those skilled workers in Canada, which this government has failed sadly to do, or we must attract skilled workers from other countries. Alternatively we can engage in a combination of these activities. We know that the situation respecting skilled workers cannot be allowed to remain as it is, because such a shortage is making it impossible for Canadian industry to increase production, and so increase the volume of goods called for by world and market demand.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that if the Minister of Finance will ease the tight money policy, and thus make it possible for those who want to increase production to obtain the funds they need to do so; and if the Minister of Labour will increase the training facilities in order to produce the additional trained personnel that this country so urgently needs; and if the Department of Citizenship and Immigration attracts the skilled workers that are so necessary, then we shall continue with the prosperity which was started and made possible by the previous government in early 1961, and which has been carried on over the past five years.
If we do not do these things, it will not be many months before this country suffers from a business downturn in exactly the same way 23033-388!

Mr. Chairman, I wish to talk about some definite points in connection with the income tax resolution. Before doing so I should like to associate myself with the remarks made earlier by my colleague the hon. member for York South, and to suggest that it is not the amount of tax that one pays that is important, but the amount one has over after one has paid taxes. I, for one, am not complaining about the tax imposed on people in our income bracket, or on those in higher brackets. I think it is important that those who have lower incomes, and who therefore cannot afford high taxes, or those who do not even have enough income to pay taxes, should be considered before those in the higher income brackets.
Having said that, I want to go on with some definite points in connection with income tax. First of all, may I say that the income tax structure in this country has been reviewed by a number of speakers tonight, and changes have been proposed. I should like to suggest several things which have not been mentioned, but which are also necessary.
The income tax structure was organized at a time when the man of the family was the sole breadwinner and when it was taken for granted that the woman would be staying home in the role of a dependant. Conditions in this country have changed very greatly, as they have in other parts of the world. We have a situation where professional women frequently, and in increasing numbers, are continuing to work after their marriage, which is advantageous from the point of view of bringing in extra income to the family.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There is, in addition, a situation in which women in the lower income brackets, many of whom have not been trained for other work, are taking jobs in industry because they need extra income in the family to make possible the purchase of the equipment and other conveniences which spell a modern

June 7, 1966
Income Tax Act
standard of living in the home. When we consider that today about 30 per cent of the Canadian labour force consists of women and that almost half of the women who work in industry are married, we are bound to realize that this is a situation which the minister should be considering in relation to the tax structure.
There are a number of changes which need to be made in the tax structure. First, the amount which a married woman is allowed to earn before deductions are made from her husband's taxable income is far too low, bearing in mind the present cost of living. The amount a married women is allowed to earn is now $250. Various organizations across Canada have requested that it be raised. I shall mention some of these organizations; they cover a wide spectrum. The most recent was the Ontario Women's Liberal Association, meeting in Toronto on May 6.

I
know they are not listening, but they will one of these days when the women of this country begin to make their demands heard. The Ontario Women's Liberal Association passed a resolution requesting that the amount be raised. Then the Canadian Horticultural Association, meeting back in February, passed a resolution on the same subject requesting that the amount a married women should be allowed to earn without interfering with her husband's exemption should be raised to $500. The Canadian Federation of University Women, who were of course thinking largely in terms of professional work, said the amount should be $950.
I wish the Minister of Finance would listen to these things. He is not hearing only one voice here tonight. These are resolutions by women's organizations, and these examples can be multiplied across the country. I have mentioned only two or three. Incidentally, I am not doing this in any feminist way. I am no feminist and I never have been in my life. I am suggesting that a large section of people has been added to the labour force both in industry and in the professions and that we shall have to reckon with this in terms of taxation policy.
The second change I would propose-and this is even more urgently demanded than the first-is that the wages of housekeepers should be deductible from the taxable incomes of mothers working outside the home. A request for this has come from individuals and from

organizations all across the country. Indeed these requests have become a regular flow.
I am glad to see there is a resolution on the order paper, No. 58, requesting that the cost of baby sitters and housekeepers be deductible as an expense for the purposes of personal income tax in the case of married working mothers engaged in certain occupations. I believe that regardless of their occupation, these people, if they are working outside the home, should be eligable for deductions in respect of home help.
Unless we make these expenses deductible it matters little how much we spend in other directions trying to keep homes intact. The homes suffer. We cannot afford situations where women, often with small children or children of school age, are not in a position to provide the help they need at home. The consequences of neglect to make such a provision are increased delinquency, irregular living habits and the lowering of moral standards.
This would be by no means the whole solution to the problem of women working outside the home. But it is one step which should be taken. People working in business are allowed to make certain costs deductible for income tax purposes. Similarly women working outside the home should have the right to deduct the expense of a housekeeper or household help. It is no use telling us that it is all very well for lawyers and businessmen to deduct such necessary expenses but that it is quite another matter for a woman working outside the home to ask for the right to make the same sort of deductions. The expenditure is just as necessary. In fact, it is more necessary because it has been established over and over again that the vast majority of women who go to work in industry do so from economic necessity, and there is no question of their being able to meet the costs of a housekeeper from outside earnings.
I wish to suggest in the third place that the salary paid to a wife employed by her husband should be treated as a separate income in the wife's hands. This would also apply to a partnership in which the wife is a member with her husband. I ask that this be allowed when the service is actually performed and the compensation is no greater than would be paid to another person for the same services. Again, this is a request which seems to be fair and reasonable. The woman is definitely contributing to building up income and should have her salary treated as if it were in her own hands.
June 7, 1966

There is a further group of people who I think should be recognized. Members of this committee have no doubt received a letter from the association known as the Single Parents Association. The members of this association represent a considerable segment of Canada's population who through unfortunate circumstances are either divorced, separated or widowed. One in every 12 families, they tell us, is a family in which a divorce has occurred. These are all men and women who are having to bear the burdens of parenthood alone. This is an unfortunate aspect of modern society which brings misery to thousands of parents and their children.
As single parents these people say that their living costs are considerably higher because it is necessary for them to hire housekeepers. Whether they be men or women, there is only one parent in the home and that parent must go out to work to earn an income. These people feel they should have broader tax exemptions to help them raise their children as educated and responsible citizens, and not as school dropouts or delinquents who in turn will create a burden on social agencies and on the taxpayers. These are problems which should be faced.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
There is another problem which is ignored in the budget and its accompanying resolutions, and that is the problem of a home in which one parent suffers a lengthy illness and the other has to go out to work. No account is taken of the expense involved in looking after the disabled parent, which necessitates the hiring of a housekeeper or of a nursing service. There are many people in these categories.
Some members of the government may have been inclined to dismiss the theory which my colleague was outlining as doctrinaire or theoretical socialism, but the government has got to the point where it knows it has to wipe out poverty, if it can do so. The only way that can be done, on the scale that it must be done, is by a wide redistribution of income in this country. People are poor, not because of cussedness or inferiority but because they have not got enough income to stay out of poverty, and they have no way of getting that income under present conditions.
I should like to summarize the points I have made. First there should be an increase in the amount which a married woman is allowed to earn before her husband's income tax exemptions are affected.
Income Tax Act
In the second place, in the case of mothers working outside the home there should be a deductible income tax allowance for the wages of a housekeeper, a baby sitter or whatever other household help is needed.
In the third place, the salary paid to a wife who is employed by her husband, or who is in a partnership, should be treated as separate income in her own hands.
In the fourth place, the case of a single parent, whether he or she be divorced, widowed, separated, income tax deductions should be permitted for the services of a housekeeper or other household help.
In the last place, but by no means the least, in the case where one parent is disabled exemptions should be permitted for housekeeping services for the care of that parent who has to remain at home.
These are problems which affect a great many Canadians and if they are solved it will stop a great many people from having to go on welfare. It is the inability to afford a housekeeper or baby sitter which prevents many married women from being able to go out and stand on their own feet and earn a living.
I have received many letters from women across the country who cannot understand why the government does not take into account the changed status of women. It is not as if this were a temporary thing and that this 30 per cent of the labour force would be going back into the home. Large numbers of married women came out of the home during the second world war to work in war plants, and have never returned on a permanent basis to the home. At least on a part-time basis they are permanently working in industry and the professions, and this factor should be recognized in our tax structure and by many departments of government. I hope the minister will take this into account, or that he has at least got to the stage of thinking about it, even though no result is apparent in these budget resolutions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday, I directed to the Prime

DEBATES	June 7, 1966
Minister (Mr. Pearson) the following question:
In view of the disastrous circumstances of the present longshoremen's strike, should the minister not take drastic and extraordinary steps so that the activity will be resumed while negotiations are under way?
It will be understood, Mr. Speaker, that this strike considerably affects my constituency and that, in short, my comments also concern the harbours of Montreal and Quebec City.
To state that it is a disastrous and catastrophic strike, Mr. Speaker, would be redundant and I will spare the house some examples which I could give in that connection.
Mr. Speaker, I think the situation has become untenable and I spent part of the day yesterday on the docks at Trois-Rivieres, talking with the longshoremen and the employers, and I repeat that the situation has become untenable.
It is not my intention to lay the blame on anyone and I should like to avoid statements likely to cast oil on the flames at a time when a settlement is being hopefully sought. But, Mr. Speaker, I should simply like, with many other members of the house, to insist by every possible means upon extraordinary measures to be resorted to, in order to settle the situation.
On this question, Mr. Speaker, I should like to note that there seems to be some differences of opinion among certain labour leaders, since Mr. Jodoin stated a few days ago-Mr. Jodoin, chairman of the C.L.C.

that he objected to compulsory arbitration and I note that a few weeks ago, the president of the United Auto Workers, an affiliate of the American Federation of Labor, and the C.I.O. was saying that this must be stopped-and I quote-it was quoted in Time, I believe.
These strikes endanger survival of society and must be stopped . . . We can no longer tolerate a situation where a group of employees, even demanding things they are entitled to, can paralyse the economy of the whole community.
It will be understood, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Reuther was not asking for compulsory arbitration unconditionally. He suggested:
A three-party commission should be set up without delay representing workers, employer and the government to evolve new systems and policies to arbitrate without delay strikes in the public service.
I think this is a case where such extraordinary measures should be taken to achieve a settlement before the economy is further affected.
June 7, 1966

Such an experiment should be made now or never.
Longshoremen are anxious to return to work, but it is understandable, of course, that they should defend their livelihood. What seems to concern them most is that the gangs are to be reduced and the workload increased. They want some protection in this connection, since they are seasonal workers.
This might also provide the house with the opportunity to look into the measures required to cope with the disadvantages of automation which will surely put a great many people out of work.
There is some talk that the Shipping Federation of Canada, allegedly connected with the British merchant marine, would not be over-anxious to settle its problem in Canada as long as the present tension exists in British ports. It seems that the federation would consider this as a fine opportunity to starve the Canadian longshoremen by extending the deadlines.
I refuse to believe in such cynicism, unless toiven proof to the contrary, but I say again that the minister should ask the house, if necessary, for the authority required to take exceptional measures for compulsory arbitration, so that the operations may be resumed before what I call a disaster is allowed to go on unduly.
We received today a release of the Shipping Federation in which it boasts of having fully co-operated with Judge Lippe. We have proof that it did not fully co-operate, since on two occasions at least, perhaps three, it declined judge Lippe's invitation to attend a conciliation meeting.
I notice in the same release that the Shipping Federation adds a thing that I consider unfair and dishonest. It says this:
During recent years, the Montreal harbour especially has gone through a period of labour unrest and has suffered Increasing losses due to thefts.
Why introduce this idea of theft when an agreement is being negotiated in that dispute? Why insinuate that longshoremen are responsible for thefts and connect them with those thefts, so as to discredit them before public opinion?
I think, Mr. Speaker, that is unfair and indicates an attitude on the part of the Shipping Federation of Canada which explains probably why it is impossible to reach an agreement in that dispute.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Mr. Speaker, I do not submit my request on behalf of the people of Trois-Rivieres only, because I know that the problem is the same in Montreal and Quebec city; however, I think it is high time for the minister to forget even those traditions calling for normal conciliation, quietly and peacefully, between workers and employers. The employers have delayed too long. A drastic measure must be taken and I can see nothing else but immediate compulsory arbitration.

Mr. Speaker, on the orders of the day last Tuesday, May 31, I put a question to the Prime Minister, which is to be found in Hansard at page 5745. It reads as follows:
Pending action on a permanent basis, will the government consider taking the necessary steps in order to use the surplus in the old age security fund to increase old age security pensions by the amount that surplus would make possible?
Mr. Speaker seemed to be of the opinion that it would be more appropriate to put this question at ten o'clock than on the orders of the day, and I agreed to do so.
It is my firm view that the day will come when the old age security pension will be increased to not less than $100 a month. I believe it should be done at this session and I hope the government will see it that way.
However, if it is going to take a bit of time to convince the government of the necessity of taking this action on a permanent basis, I suggest that temporary action be taken along
[Mr. Mackasey.i

the lines implied in my question, namely that the huge sum of money that is lying in the old age security fund be used for the purpose of increasing the old age security pension during this fiscal year.
According to table No. 53 to be found on page 163 of the budget papers that were appended to Hansard of March 29, a round figure of $215 million was to be found in the old age security fund on March 31, 1966. The surplus of receipts over expenditures during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1966, was $240 million but a $25 million transfer had been made to the consolidated revenue fund leaving in the old age security fund a surplus of $215 million. In the last fiscal year it took $923 million to pay a pension of $75 a month. If one does a bit of simple arithmetic he will find it is therefore possible to pay to the same number of people for one year an additional $17.40 a month out of the $215 million. That would be using only the surplus that is in the fund left over from last year. I suspect that the surplus in that fund is still mounting and that, all told, there is now probably enough in the fund to pay the extra $25 to bring the pension up to $100 a month.
My question is what Mr. Speaker thought it was, a suggestion that the government should follow this course. I know there are answers that the Minister of National Health and Welfare may give. If he has the time, he will no doubt quote from the speeches he is making around the country about the Canada Assistance Plan and about so-called better ways of assisting our old age pensioners; but this is something about which he and I will have to continue to disagree. I believe the only solution that is appropriate is an across-the-board increase to not less than $100 a month.
The minister may also say something about the fact that in some years the old age security fund has run a deficit and that this should be remembered in a year when there is a surplus. I remind him that I was here when we built the Old Age Security Act. We recognized at the time that we were building a plan that was on a pay-as-you-go basis. During the years when we had a deficit in the fund, that deficit was taken care of by a loan out of the general revenues of those years. In this period, the last fiscal year and this year, we are collecting from our people in the three old age security taxes more than we are paying out in pensions to our retired citizens. I suggest that in keeping with the
June 7, 1966

pay-as-you-go principle, which was the principle of the Old Age Security Act, we should use that money to increase pensions at least by the amount that surplus would make possible.
I know that the minister may use as another argument the fact there is no authority in the Old Age Security Act to use this money that is in the fund for the purpose I am suggesting. He knows, as well as I do, that there is nothing he could get through this house quicker than the necessary legislation to make it possible to use this money that is lying there to improve the position of our senior citizens.
It is not necessary, Mr. Speaker, for me to make a case in broad general terms concerning the need of our older people. It is not necessary for me to remind the house of the sympathy there is for our older people in this House of Commons. What we need is action. I know of nothing that would raise the prestige of this parliament more effectively than doing something for our senior citizens. I urge that long range action be taken as soon as possible, but in the meantime I ask the minister if he will consider seriously using the $215 million that there is in the fund by way of additional money we have collected over and above what we are paying out, to increase the pensions of our senior citizens. I say again that it could be done, on the basis of what was there last year, to the amount of $17.40 per month, and I suspect that if we used what we are now collecting by way of excess taxes, we could easily pay $25 to bring the pension to $100 a month which our senior citizens so well deserve.
