Proceedings on Adjournment Motion on behalf of the Charolais Association of Western Canada, from which I received word today. I am also glad to see the Minister of Agriculture in his seat.
The Charolais cattle in Canada and the United States are all descendants from 37 head which were imported into Mexico a number of years ago. Progeny from Mexico were sold to Canada and the United States. The Charolais Association have been in touch with me as a member representing the foothills area of Alberta, where many of the big ranches are located, in order to assist them in getting new blood into Canada for the Charolais cattle. We have not been allowed to import any because of foot and mouth disease, and restrictions which are in effect in Canada and the United States. This foot and mouth disease is not only carried by the animals but is in the semen as well. Therefore we have been unable to import these cattle up until a year and half ago, when the former minister of agriculture permitted the importation from France of 113 head.
Officials went over to France and were given permits to buy three. These were brought to Grosse Isle, near Quebec, and there kept in quarantine from October 21 of last year until quite recently. They were then moved from Grosse Isle to various parts of Canada, there to remain another 30 days in quarantine. The purpose of bringing the cattle to Canada was to cross-breed them with range cattle. The cross-bred calf, of which I have seen many, is up to 50 lbs. heavier than the ordinary heifer. Consequently that means more money in the pockets of people if they can cross breed cattle. So, the range people have wanted Charolais cattle to improve herds which have been going downhill because of inbreeding, and that sort of thing. Therefore such cattle were obtained. And for what purpose? In order to make cattle available to the breeders of Canada, and to improve Canadian herds, but not to be shipped to the United States at this time, because there is foot and mouth disease. United States buyers who are coming here and buying cattle are simply using Canada as a back door, and this government is permitting the cattle to be sent down, contrary to the spirit of the good neighbour policy.
Moreover, should foot and mouth disease break out, it would close the entire border for Canadian cattle. The United States provides the traditional market for the range men of the west.

Now there is talk of freedom of enterprise. Our buyers were permitted to buy three animals. They now say: "We want freedom of enterprise". But I will tell you this: In a matter of this kind a mistake was made by the former minister of agriculture, and the present Minister of Agriculture is perpetuating it. I have asked him, as has the association, to restrict the export of these cattle until such time as the price increases, so that the breeders in Canada can be taken care of. Let us increase the numbers of these animals in Canada, and if someone from the United States wants to buy them, let them come to Canada. If profits are to be made, let the people in Canada make them. We do not want somebody to bring them in under government supervision, quarantine and so on, and turn around the next day to make a fast buck. The man who bought the $10,000 bull in British Columbia sold a half interest for $84,000, after he left Grosse Isle to the western United States Charolais Association. Now there is talk about the traditional open door for cattle.
Certainly some people want the door kept open to our cattle. But we do not want to take the chance of foot and mouth disease going down there. Furthermore the United States has kept on its embargo on the shipment of cattle from France. We are taking a chance by bringing such cattle in here, when we may get foot and mouth disease. It may be all right to do that in Canada, but there is no reason why we should use the open door policy with respect to the United States, and get into trouble. The livestock men of the west are saying that those who want to make a fast buck out of cattle which have been brought in are doing so by using Canada as the back door to get into the United States.
A certain amount of government money was spent by the minister's going across to France. Veterinarians' expenses and things of that sort were involved. I have not totalled them up.
May I say that a resolution was unanimously passed at the directors meeting of the Charolais Cattlemen's Association in Calgary on May 31 to this effect:
The directors of the Charolais Cattle Association request a course of action to stop export of all French imported females and their female progeny until December 31, 1968 and to be reviewed at that date.

The president of the association, Mr. Ohler, took it upon himself to make a trip to Saskatoon to talk with the minister. The minister gave him the brush-off. That is my word-a straight brush-off. He passed him over to Bennett, who was his secretary. He told him he could do nothing. In other words, the former minister made a mistake. If he had said that these cattle ought to remain in Canada until such time as they could breed, there would be nothing much which could be done.
Telegrams are being sent out and I hope some helpful replies are being received. The association in the west is extremely exercised about this situation. I wish I had time to put its views on record. But I see my time is up.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
I would first commend the hon. member for his keen interest in this question. I would point out that my predecessor in this office embarked on a very sound policy, one which was pursued for the first time by reason of his dynamic leadership in this area. The first group of Charolais were brought in as a result of his incentive and keen desire to see this matter brought to a head. Along with many other good things he did, this commendable action of the minister who preceded me received all too little credit.
I would also point out to the hon. member that in my opinion some of his concern in this regard has arisen because he has not been too well informed. I know he is sincere in his protestations. Certainly from the presentation he has made here he has acquired a fine and comprehensive knowledge of the history of this breed. But as far as more recent events are concerned I do not think he is well informed. First, I would say that my department has no evidence whatsoever of any exportation of these cattle. Granted, there is nothing in the rules to prevent it. But

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion in view of the great excitement displayed by the hon. member in the house the other day I became somewhat concerned, since he seemed to feel keenly on this matter.
Accordingly I sent out the telegrams to which the hon. member has referred to see whether in fact any of these cattle are being exported. The bull to which the hon. member referred has not been exported at all. It is my understanding it is still in Canada. Americans have bought an interest in this animal, but surely this does not do any of the harm the hon. member has envisaged.
What about bull 698 and heifer 662?
I do not have the bulls by number.
They are in quarantine even if they have not been exported yet.

Let me say this to the hon. member: We sent wires to all the persons who had imported these cattle and we have received returns from about one third of them; and not a single one of them has any intention of exporting these animals.
These are the only returns we have. There is no law to prevent their being exported. My hon. friend is quite right. I do not follow his argument with respect to foot and mouth disease. These cattle have gone through a very comprehensive quarantine, as do any cattle which are imported here.
With respect to the danger of closing the border, it is certainly my view and that of the party I represent that the border should be kept as open as possible with respect to the free flow of cattle and beef both ways, just as it is now. I can think of no action more likely to close the border than for us to close it unilaterally one way for one particular breed of cattle. I think that would be very dangerous.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.38 p.m.
